## 2026-09-14 — W3R1a: an aborted admission keeps its exit ordering obligation

Reproduced GPT review finding 2 at base
`6acb5a5bf89eeabed1e89b40ad52e25bf2bdffa5`. With A's admission held,
pagehide dispatched its keepalive; admission then aborted, B committed, and
the original keepalive arrived after ordinary flushing sent B. The one- and
two-predecessor audits were **21 and 312**. Delivered keepalives applied
A/A1/A2 without a later `onWrite` settlement; dropped keepalives left only
B. All six initial reproductions failed before the implementation changed.

The exit transport now records exactly the prefix it is about to dispatch,
before calling fetch. That record is independent of the pending-admission
map. The ordinary sender reconciles its original mutation ids, arguments and
minted row ids before sending a successor; repeated exits select that same
unresolved head. A successful admission keeps the ordinary durable outbox.
If admission fails, the web host keeps the fallback for the document's
lifetime, including close/reopen of the same store in that document. A new
document cannot recover an admission and keepalive that were both lost;
the existing loss control now explicitly destroys its modeled document.
The client also rechecks the exposed head after asynchronous queue reads,
so a previously captured durable queue cannot bypass a newly exposed write.

A `failed` response alone is not always a terminal receipt: input validation
can refuse before recording the id. An exposed failure therefore needs a
replay-confirmed refusal before successors proceed. A recorded refusal
releases the successor, even if the original delayed keepalive arrives
later. Unknown replies and retryable unrecorded failures retain the head.
Known receipts retired on store replacement also remove their exposure
record, preserving LLP 3000.007 §18.2's existing identity fence.

An exposed admission failure now returns retryable `E_EXIT_ADMISSION` and
later settles through `onWrite` with the same id while the client is open.
The writes card and README explain that this does not promise non-application
and that the caller must not resubmit with a fresh id. If retaining the
ordering record itself fails, sticky `E_EXIT_ORDER` stops the page's
mutation sending, including when admission also aborts. Both codes are in
`guide::CODES`. Their messages are:

- `E_EXIT_ADMISSION`: `admission failed after this write was exposed at exit; its server outcome is unknown and this page will retry the same id before later writes`
- `E_EXIT_ORDER`: `exit write ordering could not be preserved; this page has stopped sending writes`

The old admission exception used `E_STORE` and the interpolated message
`write ${id} admission outcome is unknown: ${String(error)}`, without a
retryable flag or later settlement obligation. Unexposed admission failures
retain that existing behavior. No client card type, server route, meter
ceiling, serialized value, corpus case or application caller changed.

The final thirteen regressions cover six delivery/admission interleavings,
four unresolved-receipt controls (retryable/unrecorded, with/without a
same-page reopen), two record-preservation failures (admission commits or
aborts), and a recorded terminal refusal that releases B. An isolated
generated package with the three client implementation files taken from the
exact base above fails all thirteen; the final implementation passes all
thirteen. That comparison uses `/tmp` only, no alternate checkout or commit.
Two additional defects found during implementation were made red before
repair: an unrecorded failure releasing successors (two controls plus the
terminal-receipt positive control, 0/3), and an admission abort masking the
stop-sending refusal as E_STORE (0/1). Both are green in the final run.

Final six-case measurements, in delivered/dropped/delayed order, one then
two predecessors: recovery **17/28/18/25/1013/1021 ms**; application orders
**12/123/12/123/12/123**; applications **2/3/2/3/2/3**; ordinary sends and
sent settlements **2/3/2/3/2/3**; **0 duplicate applications** after the
original delayed keepalive completes. The failed callers receive **1/2**
later sent settlements. Record-preservation refusals send **0** exit and
**0** ordinary requests. The existing bounds remain **65,536 bytes** shared
keepalive bodies, **32 writes** per batch and a **1,000 ms** exit wait.

## 2026-09-14 — W3R2: source-owned removal markers and source-located prediction notes

Base: `f675e01d7b53d15144aef528e650c38b8a7ba6b1` (wave-3 integration HEAD, on lane branch `sb4/w3r2`). No commit, push, tag or publication. Read the Grok review at
`/Users/ccheever/projects/snapback-w3-review/grok.md`, W3b2 and W3R1f above,
the Snapback 4 fence and exclusions, `rules/RULES.md`, LLP 3000 §6–§7,
and LLP 3000.007 §5.6, §14, §18, §20.3 and §20.4 with `llp-orient`.

**Built.** The feeds card and README require a tombstone's actor to be the
viewer, its ID to equal its event ID, and the existing source event to be
owned by that viewer. The source check uses the total unique `posts.byId`
key plus its actor equality. The tombstone's `eventId` is an opaque `id`:
Quarry refuses equality between nominal references to two different tables,
so the rule proves the cross-table identity and existence explicitly. No
value serialization or engine authority changes. `removeEvent` remains the
only published tombstone insert, called by `deletePost` and `unrepost`,
before deleting the source in the same transaction. Private inbox rules,
source residency, purge bounds and null-slot pagination keep their contract.

The language Following example points to the full feeds recipe for removal
and null slots. Grouped `N_NOT_PREDICTABLE` lists retain distinct roots and
rewrites and show source `file:line:col`, including inserts and deletes in
expanded helpers. Read IR paths were already translated on this base; the
remaining synthetic write labels and helper-delete header fallback reproduced.
The binder records write source occurrences in its existing side map and
records the helper delete's point source. Lowered IR and execution decisions
are unchanged. No new diagnostic or note code was added.

LLP 3000.007 §20.4 now states the shipped writes-card contract: durable
oldest-head retry, the ordered pre-admission best-effort prefix, the shared
65,536-byte / 32-write caps, the one-second retry wait, and the writes that
can still be lost before admission. The Chromium after-results were already
journaled by the lead; this lane did not rerun them. The forbidden client
files `local.ts`, `local-exit.ts` and `web.ts` were not changed.

**Regression worlds and numbers.** On the exact base above, a forged marker
was accepted and changed the victim's Following on all three hosts: server,
memory device and SQLite device. With the rule fixed, the marker is refused
`E_RULE`, the victim's page is identical, no private row changes, and a
purge has zero rows to delete. There are five server attack variants in two
worlds each: the copied implicit-ID insert, an explicit matching foreign ID,
a forged actor, the real actor with the wrong marker ID, and a missing source.
Their complete observation compares first/retry bodies, receipt, all seven
meters, committed delta, effects, attacker snapshot/stream and admission,
reopen and settlement on both stores. Each pair differs only in a private
copy's event identity, which the victim can read and the attacker cannot.

Two separately named device tests each run both worlds. They hold a victim
device through the attack, its stream and a no-op purge, and hold an attacker
device through admission, reopen and failed settlement. Prediction changes
from true on the base to false: the source ownership probe is online-only,
so admission queues without a tombstone. Every world includes the positive
control: the real owner can still remove the event, hide the target copy,
and have the system purge it without deleting the other world's different
event. Existing ordinary/repost/promotion/envelope and cut tests pass.

The changed-note fixture remains **3 notes / 7 distinct root causes**;
synthetic insert/delete/upsert site labels fall from **7 to 0**, and the two
helper-delete header fallbacks become the helper's actual line. The existing
full-envelope regression still tests **1,000 people / 50,000 events**; the
1,001-copy purge body measures **1,003 examined / 6,009 index entries /
0 rule probes / 6,016 steps / 988,196 heap bytes / 6 output bytes /
1,002 rows written**. No meter ceiling was raised.

**What the implementation taught.** A typed reference checks shape, not
source existence or ownership. The table rule must enforce ownership even
when the paved helper already checks it. The first attempted equality used

## 2026-09-14 — W3R3e: cut authorization is unknown; a later heap cut still unwinds

Base: `96d5be3bc95523e3b3abd388265fab7cbd85bd62`. Read findings A and D in

entry and `git show bb28c8716`. Used `llp-orient` for the Snapback 4 fence,

and README supplied the current surface. No commit, push, tag or publication.

**Built.** A metered rule probe unwinds as unknown before `not` or a
short-circuit operator can use a false sentinel. For a capped point read,
the rule's schema-derived worst-case probe count must fit before looking
for the target. If it cannot, both hidden and absent worlds record the same
cut and unwind to null/incomplete/no continuation; a hidden denial cannot
restore that cut away. With room, the existing probe charges and hidden/miss
normalization remain. System authority and trusted synced reads need no
probe allowance. Writes and predictions still use `Cut::Abort`; this new
point check applies only to `Cut::Cap`.

The runner also unwinds a query's heap bound when the first recorded cut
used another meter. The first cut remains recorded. The unknown-lookup
unwind, heap-first behavior, mutation rollback, step-limit refusal and live
aggregate partial-count contract remain. Production changes are confined to
`engine/read.rs` and one condition in `engine/runner.rs`; no meter ceiling,
serialized form, existing corpus case, parser form, code or note changed.
The reads card, README and LLP 3000.007 §17 state the final rule.

## 2026-09-14 — W3R3c: confirmed exposed writes settle; permanent refusals release the queue

Reproduced re-check findings B and C against base
`96d5be3bc95523e3b3abd388265fab7cbd85bd62` before changing implementation.
Both acquisition-persistence interleavings (abort before commit and lost
response after commit) applied A but lost its `sent` notification after
its caller received `failed/E_EXIT_ADMISSION`. Both permanent-refusal client
cases left B waiting: a removed operation and an argument narrowed from
200 characters to 1. The real HTTP tests separately reproduced missing
receipts for a removed operation, typed argument bounds, and wire decoding.
The last two are different paths: the engine's input validator also returned
an unrecorded failure after HTTP decoding succeeded.

The client retains the exposure record through local receipt persistence
and notification. A confirmed exposed outcome resolves and emits `onWrite`
before the following acquisition, with no await between notification and
removing the exposure. If receipt persistence or close interrupts that path,
the retained exposure remains replayable even when its durable outbox entry
already has a sent sequence. Ordinary, unexposed successful writes keep their
existing sync-before-notification timing. No new durable format or public
card word was introduced; the fallback's lifetime is still this document.

The server now finalizes write-specific operation and argument refusals in
the existing principal/mutation-id receipt store, for individual and ordered
batch requests. The helper rechecks the id in the same transaction that
records the failure, so a concurrent applied receipt wins. Engine input
validation uses it too. The first failure keeps its existing diagnostic
message; replay uses the existing value-free receipt message. A receipt
survives restart and a restored operation definition: a delayed request or
corrected arguments under that id cannot execute later. A valid successor
and the same id under another principal can still execute. Authentication
and retryable transport/store refusals remain unrecorded and retryable.
The writes card and README state terminal failure replay and notification
independence from sync persistence.

Measured acceptance: each B case has **1** failed caller, **1** injected apply
persistence failure, **1** later sent settlement, **1** server application,
and **0** duplicates. Each C case has **1** terminal failure settlement and
**1** sent successor, ordinary request ids **A, A, B** (**3** sends), audit
order **2**, and **0** duplicates after the delayed original request returns
`failed` with `replayed: true`. The HTTP tests cover both routes across
**3** permanent refusal classes and **1** restart per class after refusal,
plus same-principal finality and another-principal success. The affected
client run includes the existing transient retry/hold controls.

## 2026-09-15 — W4b: Following checks tombstones inside the merge

Base: `118de1c72dd53801426ba2660e12151eca0c1ee8` (`sb4/w4b`, 0.2.19).
Used `llp-orient` for the Snapback 4 fence, LLP 3000 §6–§7 and
LLP 3000.007 §5.6, §14, §18 and §20.12; read the feeds card, README,
wave-3 GPT finding 1, re-check A/D/N1 and the reverted W3R1f/W3R3e entries.
No commit, push, tag, publication, sub-agent or remote machine.

**Built option 1.** The Following recipe returns a merge with
`where not exists removedEvents[eventId = .eventId]` in its header.
The parser previously stopped at the index and required `:`; its AST,
parser, binder and printer now carry the optional predicate. The binder
lowers it to each lane's existing filtered scan, binding `.` to that lane's
row. Plain, named-table and matching merges use the same predicate typing,
helper setup and metered reads as an ordinary filtered scan; existing
named-table and matching restrictions remain. This is a language addition,
not just a binder refusal removed. No engine, read-rule evaluation, meter,
ceiling, serialized value/IR form or existing corpus case changed. No new
diagnostic code or note was added, so `guide::CODES` is unchanged.

**What the existing engine proves.** `scan_prepared` checks `capped_at`
after the predicate and before pushing its row. A cut therefore stops before
an unchecked candidate; previously checked live rows can remain. The
existing eager and lazy merge paths suppress `next` on a meter cut.
A direct filtered scan instead positions after its last rule-visible
examined key, including the candidate whose public predicate cut: the new
direct-scan control returns r0, positions after r1, then reaches r2. That
existing direct-scan rule is unchanged. A cursor-bearing uniform filtered
merge is complete at its page size within budget, or the end. A merge
without a cursor still reports incomplete when more matches exist; the
README and feeds card explicitly retain this distinction.

The feeds card and README now return live rows without null slots, filling
through removed candidates under the existing meter. The language card
exercises a merge predicate and points to the full tombstone recipe.
LLP 3000.007 §20.12 replaces the cut-lookup residual with this result.
Existing W3R2 authority assertions now expect empty pages instead of null
slots; their private-world comparisons, failed forgery/reopen/settlement,
legitimate owner removal and purge remain. Pagination also reuses a cursor
acquired before removal and verifies the 20-row live page plus its 3-row
terminal page. The purge and 1,000-person / 50,000-event controls pass.

**Measurements (deterministic counters, not latency claims).** Seed 40
pushed events above the fixture's 3 originals; remove the newest 20.
The device checks install the reader's actual snapshot into each real
DeviceStore and call the shared local interpreter with test ceilings,
because the public device dispatcher fixes them. Ordinary dispatcher,
stream and durable-store authority controls also pass.

| Host | Ceiling | Examined before → after | Removed IDs/bodies before → after | Complete before → after | Next before → after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| Server | 25 | 42 → 26 | 17 → 0 | false → false | true → false |
| Memory device | 25 | 42 → 26 | 17 → 0 | false → false | true → false |
| SQLite device | 25 | 42 → 26 | 17 → 0 | false → false | true → false |

Before, 41 of the 42 examined ceilings leaked and 20 carried unsafe
continuations, on each host. After, every ceiling from 1 through the
uncut cost of 82 excludes removed IDs and bodies, with zero cut cursors:
246 swept queries across the hosts. The uncut page changes from 20 null
slots at 42 examinations to 20 live rows at 82 examinations and 41
predicate probes, keeping a continuation. The higher cost fills through
20 removed events and includes a live lookahead; it does not raise a meter.
The equivalent removal-page control measures 0 index entries, 191 steps,
18,078 heap bytes, 5,331 output bytes and 0 writes. Purging three removed
events takes 3 chunks and writes 21 rows for 5 followers, 904 for 900.

**N1 before and after.** A non-uniform read rule probes permits by each
record's owner. The hidden world has 20 protected records and the absent
world none, with the same public grant and sequence. Plain scan, filtered
scan and scan-then-unconditional-refusal run across examined ceilings 1–82,
with rule-probe ceilings 0 and the default. Compare every viewer response
field, including errors, cursor, dependencies, sequence and expiry; operator
meter fields stay off this comparison as they stay off the wire. All 492
pairs per host match, before and after: 1,476 pairs per revision, with
6 visible-row positive controls. Device N1 installs adversarial online-only
rows deliberately to reach the read-rule path; it is not a sync claim.
For the final before run, all six changed language source/card files were
temporarily restored byte-for-byte from the base, the core and those files
were checked with `git diff --exit-code`, then the saved changes restored.
The original cut regressions were already red before any production edit.

**What I learned.** Moving the check into the existing scan boundary is
enough; a new engine-wide unknown value is unnecessary and would reopen the
reverted work's disclosure-sensitive paths. Options 2 and 3 were not needed.
The trade is bounded refill work and no continuation when that work cuts;
a caller retries its cursor after cleanup. Round-2 A's raw point-read
rule-probe issue is outside this fix. No out-of-scope file was touched.
Every changed code file is below 1,500 lines (largest: guide.rs, 1,364).

## 2026-09-15 — W4a: synchronous admission custody across immediate web navigation

Built against `118de1c72dd53801426ba2660e12151eca0c1ee8` (0.2.19).
The Node model now destroys the document before the admission save completes,
with both same-turn teardown and an explicitly held save, one and two writes.
Its real wasm device and real server run a non-idempotent application counter
and decimal order audit. The four regressions failed on that unchanged base:
zero applications after reopen. They pass with the synchronous journal.

`web.ts` receives `call({ op: "admit", ... })` synchronously inside `mutate`,
before its first await, so this lane needs no change to `local.ts`,
`local-exit.ts`, the server, or the public client card. `web-journal.ts`
captures the operation, mutation id, arguments, minted row ids, viewer, time
and submission order in localStorage. I chose localStorage because its
synchronous `setItem` completes in that call stack and its same-origin
contents survive navigation. The claimed device-store name (including the
existing tab suffix) and backend store identity scope each journal key.
The captured JSON is also the ordinary admission's body, so a caller changing
its arguments after `mutate` returns cannot change that write.

On open, journal records enter the existing outbox through ordinary device
admission, in order before new writes. A surviving page whose save fails also
recovers older records before its next admission. Live admissions stay with
their original calls, preserving their typed refusal outcomes. The ordinary
outbox is the only sender: no new server route, unadmitted keepalive, terminal
server receipt, or exposure tracking exists. There is no new ordering
obligation between sends: the journal creates no send, and the existing
outbox serializes every recovered write with its original mutation id.

An IDB transfer marker (`j`, private to the web host and never loaded into
wasm) commits atomically with admission. It records only local transfer and
origin, not a server result or terminal outcome. If localStorage removal
fails, the marker dedupes the id even after its outbox receipt has retired;
it is collected once cleanup succeeds. Locally refused prediction and
validation remove the record and return the ordinary failure. Self-review
found that saving a marker for an already-known refusal could mask it as
`E_STORE` during an IDB outage; a red regression drove synchronous refusal
cleanup before that bookkeeping, preserving `WRONG_DIGIT`.

Closed tabs use the existing Web Lock and orphan adoption rule. Live-tab
journals are not adopted. The brief's literal "never sent to a replaced
backend" is stricter than §18.2's existing rule for already-admitted unknown
outbox writes: recovered, previously unadmitted writes retain their source
identity until retirement, and an authenticated replacement removes them
without a send. Ordinary already-admitted writes retain §18.2's behavior.
The tests cover an immediate mismatch, replacement discovered from the
server, and an offline recovery followed by replacement. A same-store
restore still uses the existing halt.

Bounds are **65,536 bytes per serialized record**, **262,144 bytes of UTF-8
keys and values per device journal**, and **32 records**. Over-budget writes,
unavailable/throwing/full localStorage, an unidentified backend, and browser
storage clearing retain best-effort unawaited navigation; ordinary admission
still runs without a synchronous throw. A journal-only write needs another
client to open. The README, writes card and LLP 3000.007 §20.4 state these
limits and keep `await client.mutate(...)` as the strongest durable boundary.
This is a navigation model, not physical-power-loss or real-Chromium evidence.

Measurements from the final affected run:

- One-write same-turn/held-save recovery: **1/1 applications**, order **1/1**,
  **17/18 ms**, **609/609 journal-value bytes**.
- Two-write same-turn/held-save recovery: **2/2 applications**, order **12/12**,
  **35/22 ms**, **1,218/1,218 journal-value bytes**.
- **0 duplicate applications** in all four; original minted row ids preserved.
- Surviving-journal controls, queued and retired receipt: **1 admission,
  1 send, 1 application, 0 duplicates** each.
- UTF-8 record control: **56,612-byte record** journaled, **56,758 bytes**
  including its key; the oversized record falls back and **2/2 writes apply**.
- Total-byte control: **4 of 5 records** journaled, **227,032 bytes** including
  keys; **5/5 writes apply**. Count control: **32 of 33 records** journaled,
  **24,279 bytes**; **33/33 writes apply**.
- Closed-tab recovery plus successor: **3 applications**, order **123**.
  A still-locked tab: **0 applications** from adoption, then **1** from its owner.
- Replacement controls: **0 sends, 0 applications** across all **3** cases.

## 2026-09-15 — W4R1b: merge predicate discovery bindings and Following review coverage

**Base:** `b1b9fd9ec364fcebd74caf20f533759ae9a99521` (`sb4/w4r1b`).
No commit, push, tag or publication. No engine, read-rule probe, point-read,
meter ceiling or serialized-value change; no other lane's client file touched.

**Built.** Finding A reproduced on the server, memory device and SQLite
device: the first page omitted `dev:a-00` (red) and included `dev:a-01`
(blue), because lazy discovery left the B/blue selector in the environment.
The binder now initializes each filtered discovery lane's selector through
its existing setup. Nonempty setup selects eager evaluation, keeping that
selector live through the lane's complete scan. This is a conservative
fallback for all filtered discovery lanes, including helpers; it avoids a
new dependency walker or runtime environment. Uniform fixed-prefix filtered
lanes on one seekable plain index and unfiltered discovery lanes remain lazy.
Following's named inbox/broadcast merge remains eager, even with no pulls.
The new fixture compares the natural path with forced eager execution and
an equivalent fixed-prefix lazy query, including cursors, completeness,
exact expected IDs, tied ordering keys and termination. The wanted rows are
**48**, in **3 pages (20, 20, 8)** on every host; the unfiltered control is
**96 rows / 5 pages**. Both direct `p.wanted` and helper expansion are covered.

**Costs and cuts (B, C, missing coverage).** The ordinary fixture now pins
**82 examinations / 41 tombstone probes** and ceiling **25** to empty data,
`complete: false`, no `next`. The promoted fixture starts with 5 followers,
writes the pushed events, really promotes on follower **51**, and adds a
live broadcast that must appear in the uncut first page. It pins **85
examinations / 42 probes**. Across server, memory and SQLite, the respective
**1..=82 / 1..=85** sweeps find **0 removed IDs/bodies** and **0 unsafe cut
cursors**; ceiling 25 returns **0 rows** in both shapes. Promotion matters:
`removeEvent` deletes a shared broadcast immediately, so seeding only shared
posts and deleting them would skip the long inbox tombstone run.

The N1 helper adds a merge predicate using `exists records[...]` against a
non-uniform-rule table. It compares `data`, `complete`, `next`, `seq`,
`tables`, `nextExpiry` and refusal fields between hidden and absent worlds,
under **82 examined ceilings × 2 probe ceilings × 4 forms = 656 pairs per
host**, all identical, with **4 positive controls per host**. Device tests
explicitly install adversarial online-only rows to exercise rules; this
is interpreter/store evidence, not an assertion that those rows sync.
The heap regression cuts at **20 bytes** while allocating the second
tombstone key, after **26 bytes charged / 3 examinations / 1 probe**;
all three hosts return **null data**, incomplete and no cursor. Default
budgets return **20 live rows** and a continuation. Cost, examined-cut,
non-uniform and heap coverage passed the base implementation before the
binder fix; no new engine fix was needed for those missing tests.

## 2026-09-15 — cursor continuation gain replicates on native Linux

The fixed 0.2.18 ignored candidate completed the second-platform comparison
on Ubuntu 24.04 / native AMD EPYC 9454. Native qualification passes 368
candidate and eight baseline selected Rust test executions, including four
full outcome/refusal equality cases. All 117,000 formal timed HTTP calls,
7,020 excluded warmups, 162 untimed walks / 33,510 pages and 24 physical
proofs pass. Fresh Linux guest sessions remain unchanged through live
leave/regrant; all 42 recorded child groups stop with expected exits.

All twelve continuation cases improve median p50, ten p95 and eleven rate;
29/36 paired p50s improve. The 150-group rotating feed at eight clients
falls 3.292→2.849 ms p50 and 4.802→4.134 ms p95, with throughput
2,214.4→2,659.8 requests/s. This replicates the continuation median gain
with the same cursor/runtime and differential-test overlays used on Darwin.

The tails remain mixed: 150-group next-page C8 p99 rises 4.738→11.260 ms,
and first-page p50/rate medians worsen at both C1/C8. Five-group next-page
C8 also loses p95/p99/rate. The complete record preserves 80 median and 264
paired losses across six metrics, the one median tie and twelve RSS points.
After-workload RSS medians rise 260 KiB, with mixed paired differences.
No host-isolation, memory-pressure, current-package or competitor claim is
made. This experiment changes neither current core source nor package.

Both unchanged calculators pass their first formal execution and agree on
all raw values, medians, contrasts, counts/losses/ties and RSS. The independent
calculator froze before formal result access, after launch and the first
baseline completion; its original stale timing statement is corrected by a
preserved annotation. The pre-freeze wrapper mismatch and failed initial
staging/observation attempts remain recorded without relabeling failures.
The successful formal workload was never restarted.

Six full original formal records are appended to storage.jsonl. The existing
benchmark README and core-owner issue retain the native build, setup,
protocol, source/binary bindings, results and limitations. Second-platform
replication is complete; evaluate the tail/first-page tradeoffs with the core
owner before adoption and measure current competitors separately. The
broader performance goal remains open.

## 2026-09-15 — W5e: scheduled Trending preserves like prediction (G5, M2; S25)

Built option 2 from the lane brief, on base
`2862bfdadd6cf846029628151d2fb6a39006d2ed`. The investigation of LLP
3000.007 §20.9 found that D1's refusal is necessary for the existing value
index reader. The expiry sweep already subtracts physical contributions
transactionally with target/index/log changes. Before the sweep, live reads
recompute contributions, but scan candidates and cursor keys are selected
in physical order first. Counts can lose their stored winner; a sum can
gain a winner when a negative contribution expires. Checking only winners
cannot restore the order or continuation. A bounded full live fold/sort
remains the immediate-query alternative; a new expiry reindexing or ranked
read protocol is not claimed. Device horizons and independent clocks give
no additional proof that the stored rank is current.

The feeds card now has a complete scheduled Trending recipe. `create`
writes only its post; `like`/`unlike` write only the viewer's private source
row, with an online-only non-expiring `likeCounts` maintained as an engine
side effect. The system schedule alone writes `ranked`; application insert,
update and delete there are denied. There is no `posts.score` or
`update <- allow`. Ranking is like count, post time, id, including zero-like
posts. The window is explicitly posts younger than 24 hours, not recent
likes on arbitrarily old posts. Scores and new candidates lag by one
one-minute period when the job runs promptly; queue, chunk and sync delay
add latency, and chunks do not form an atomic ranking snapshot. Candidate
expiry at post time plus 24 hours is live on every host before a sweep.
The immediate card query is now `trendingNow`; both existing card consumers
were updated. The expiry/maintains cards, README, diagnostic registry and
governing RFC record the same limits. The README's stale claim that live
counts wait for the sweep is corrected.

Measured in deterministic tests, not a production throughput benchmark:
105 candidates, 11 pages of at most 10, two 100-post chunks per scoring pass;
60,000 ms cadence and 59,999 ms observed like-to-score lag. A like writes
two total rows (source and maintained count), zero ranked rows, and leaves
the author's post unchanged. Each device store predicted 4/4 like-state
operations (like, repeat, unlike, like) and 1/1 create; zero ranked overlay
writes. Authoritative delivery settled all five queued writes and delivered
score 1. Boundary tests cover candidate expiry before/after the sweep and
future-post admission. The retained immediate-query regressions find the
correct winners among 1,500 candidates (3,000 examinations), and report
incomplete at 8,193 candidates (16,385 charged examinations including nested
reads and the refused charge). No meter ceiling or serialized value changed.

Regression proof before the recipe/rewrite: language 0 passed / 1 failed,
simulator 0 / 2, device 0 / 2. Afterward: the same language filter 1 / 0;
guide 23 / 0 and maintains 6 / 0; simulator 2 / 0; device 2 / 0; repairs
9 / 0. The initial card attempt had guide 22 / 1 because public subset sync
was refused; the final recipe uses the viewer's own read audience. The
largest changed code file is 1,458 lines.


The prediction card and README now explain the tradeoffs: a viewer-keyed
rule, no horizon and viewer-covered caps can predict, but only the viewer's
reactions are readable; full public sync covers a per-message cap but
publishes everyone's reactions. There is also an existing membership path:
include the conversation in every unique key and cap group, remove the
horizon, and hold the positive membership witness. The existing device test

reaction in the conversation. Neither changing to `insert if absent` nor
adding an existence branch proves that only the children of a held message
are complete. Pending guidance uses the existing write `state` and

covered cap predict 1 row each; horizon and uncovered cap predict 0.
No ceiling, serialized value form or upsert runtime rule changes. The CLI's

(0 passed, 3 failed) and green after (3 passed, 0 failed). The nullable-key
regression is separately red (0 passed, 1 failed); the final insert-arm

Design note, not built: preserving Clique's message horizon requires a
parent-linked complete child group. For every held message, acquisition
would need to deliver all its reactions at one snapshot/stream boundary,
not an independent last-500 slice. A schema-enforced parent relation must
bind the child's conversation to that message; the held membership witness
then proves readability for the key and insert image. Every secondary
unique population and the full `cap 50 by messageId` population must lie
inside that complete child group, and group revocation/reacquisition must
withdraw/restore its proof together with the rows. An empty local lookup
under today's last-500 reaction horizon cannot distinguish no reaction
from an older reaction omitted at acquisition; a cap is only a population
bound, not evidence that its population arrived. The smallest sound
extension is this parent-linked complete-child acquisition rule with its
schema relation and lifecycle, using the membership proof that already
exists. Removing the independent child horizon alone does not establish
the parent dependency or bound acquisition to held messages. No such
extension is implemented in this lane.

Final review extended the initial 6-line runtime guard to 10 added lines:
only an id minted by this operation can bypass the primary-key absence
proof. A caller-supplied id on a private table must prove that key too.
The fixed-id control was red (0 passed, 1 failed) before that correction;
the final if-absent test is green (1 passed, 0 failed) across 6 shapes on
both stores, with matching diagnostic headings: 6 predicted admissions
(1 row each) and 6 queued admissions (0 rows each). Public supplied-id
inserts remain eligible. The compiler keeps literal/default image facts
and its single-assignment snapshots, without executing expressions.

requires the author to choose its value; the diagnostic prints the complete
order and does not mechanically discard one. Merge and chunk headers retain
their existing grammar.

The predicate parser now treats a modifier at the `where` expression's level
as the end of that predicate, belonging to the outer read. Thus
`posts['bob'] where exists follows[viewer, .author] after c last 1 by byAuthor`
reads the outer page, without extracting a helper. Parentheses (or a call's
argument delimiters) start a separate expression scope: an inner read with
its own modifiers is `(exists follows[viewer, .author] by byPair)`.
This is a precedence rule, not a guessed reassignment based on index names;
there is no refusal or mechanical rewrite for an input the grammar now
binds unambiguously. Cursor continuation is exercised on actual rows.

A declared shape at the scalar tail of a predicate shapes the outer page,
including unary and conditional predicates, nested probes, loop domains and
shapes declared in another file. `where not .hidden card` and the explicit
spread wrapper compile to the same IR. A valid row/object shape inside a
predicate keeps its existing meaning; parentheses make that scope explicit,
and `{ ...card }` explicitly selects the page. The binder checks the tail's
type in an isolated copy so speculative setup, source sites and notes do not
leak. The old scalar-shape refusal and CLI wrapper repair were deleted.

A positional key with exactly one full unique-index candidate selects it in
both program reads and table-rule probes. Explicit `by` still wins. Zero or
multiple unique candidates keep the ambiguity refusal and mechanical index
selection. Because diagnostics print canonical modifier order, the CLI's
index repair now also reparses the read span to recognize reordered modifiers
and parenthesized keys, preserving the author's source order and comments.

The existing field interpreter already propagates null and evaluates its base
once. Consequently the smallest meaning-preserving optional-chaining repair
is to remove the `?`, producing `a.b`, including for a call or point read.
The diagnostic explains that fact and marks the token rewrite mechanical.
The old conditional rewrite could repeat the base; it and its obsolete
matching branch were removed. Actual CLI round trips retain parentheses,
comments and string literals. This changes no runtime semantics or serialized
forms. Reading the member binder and the interpreter's null branch exposed
this simpler answer; a new optional-field form or helper rewrite was unnecessary.
The language card, reads card, code explanation and package README describe
the accepted forms; the language card's thread now uses them and still runs.

## 2026-09-15 — W5R1x: replay ownership and bounded write receipts

Built from `0246023537b31baed75e06ef08ffdba1621bf49e`, without a commit,
push, tag or publication. A persistent dev host now holds the existing
`serve.lock` at the resolved store directory before opening its engine;
deploy, rollback and release serving already use that lock. Competing hosts
on the same or different ports refuse before changing replay or schedule
metadata. Binding also precedes policy changes, so an unrelated occupied
port does not release a stopped replay's policy. Dev policy writes check
release identity transactionally, including a delayed dev engine opened
before activation. Release startup leaves dev policy alone. The engine
carries its development/release mode into mutation, Quarry-job and native-job
effect recording; release engines ignore suppression metadata, and a
transactional release-identity check also fences a stale dev engine.

Terminal write history and event deduplication now retain at most 256 ids;
pending writes are independent of the bound. Device receipts use one bounded
metadata record, with insertion and eviction in the same device transaction,
so two native owners cannot lose each other's retained receipts through a
read/overwrite race. Receipt persistence still precedes executable outbox
retirement. Both device stores use the same implementation. Closed web-tab
adoption merges that bounded history before removing the source store.
`client.write(id)` returns undefined after terminal eviction; the README
and writes card state the bound, the durable window and pending retention.
This replaces the per-id receipt format rather than adding a compatibility
lane. The existing React early-outcome map already caps at 256 and needed
no change; the online client inherits the shared history fix.

The opener and acquisition findings were already correct behavior. Six
new tests passed before changes: on wasm and process devices, a transient
fetch failure returns the open client with acquisition false and link
offline; replacement remains unacquired until its new catch-up finishes;
and a same-store restore halt stays unacquired across retry and offline
reopen. The starter comments, README and writes card now explain the
close-and-throw contract. The public `sync()` resolves without a value;
its internal sync routine returns false on fetch failure. The public
`acquired` flag is the readiness authority.

## 2026-09-15 — W5R2a: one durable receipt window, destination-first adoption

Built from `79013faea0ebd4cf1471974b25f9f1f25509662c` for wave 5's final
receipt-history review round. Kept durable recovery; the session-only fallback
was not needed. Local clients now read server receipts directly from the one
256-entry device metadata record and pending state from the current executable
outbox. There is no second in-memory server-receipt window, persisted-id list,
or pending-write cache to evict independently or to resurrect after another
native owner settles a write. The existing session-only pre-admission refusals
remain bounded to 256; online/mock history keeps its existing session contract.
A mutation's waiting callback is released when its promise returns, including
when it returns pending; later terminal events do not need that callback.

`keep_write` accepts one new completion or an adopted older window. Adoption
unions by id in the device transaction, keeps destination values on collisions,
and places the destination after the incoming entries before trimming to 256.
The web host transfers the orphan's window in one call and persists the result
before removing the orphan. An orphan can fill spare capacity, never displace
what the destination already holds. The stored receipt format is unchanged.

Event ids follow the executable outbox snapshot the client already reads;
there is no independently evicting 256-id server-event list. A sent entry's
receipt was persisted before settlement, so repeated flushing, opening or
retirement on replacement does not reinsert that receipt after eviction.
A flush that already knows the terminal receipt skips its event. Reads may
still report sent while the terminal outbox entry exists; after both the
receipt and entry leave, they return undefined. The README and writes card
state these rules. No new diagnostic or note was introduced.

Before implementation all five new client regressions failed. Two native
owners exercised 600 device-protocol settlements (the second owner writes the
receipt, settles and removes the outbox entry): durable history stayed at 256,
but the observing history retained 600 pending values. Afterward the same
measurement is 256 durable receipts, 0 cached pending values, 0 cached server
outcomes, and 0 outbox entries; the newest 256 remain sent and evicted ids are
undefined. On both wasm and process devices, one real sent write held in the
outbox followed by 256 local refusal emissions fired its event twice before,
once after. The final regression also fills the durable window with 256 other
receipts before flushing: the queued id remains sent, emits once, does not
refresh its evicted receipt, and becomes undefined after catch-up removes it.

The web tests use a full 256-receipt orphan window, including one colliding id.
Before, destination windows of 256 and 128 retained only that one overlapping
id. After, all 256/256 and 128/128 destination receipts remain readable before
and after reopen; adoption contributes 0 and 128 receipts respectively, with
256 total in either case and the destination's original collision value.
The Rust scenario runs on SQLite and memory with destination sizes 0, 128 and
256, and checks filling, collisions, ordering, repeat adoption, ordinary new
completion eviction and reopen. This is device/window evidence, not a claim
about physical power loss or 600 server executions.

## 2026-09-15 — W5R2b: mint facts survive statements that cannot assign the alias

N2 reproduced against `79013faea0ebd4cf1471974b25f9f1f25509662c`:
`chosen = new`, followed by an unrelated `require`, made the binder report
that an insert-if-absent could not predict. Both device stores still predicted
one row through the fully held private table's `(postId, principal)` unique
key. Reads, emits, other writes, and non-assigning branches and loops had the
same mismatch: six forms, 12 binder/runtime mismatches across SQLite and
memory. The regression uses the base implementation with the final tests;
its supplied-id and reassignment controls already agreed with the runtime.

The insert residency tracker now retains mint facts across unrelated
statements. A direct binding replaces only its own fact and can establish a
new mint or copy an existing mint alias. Branches and loops recursively
invalidate only names they may write, including nested bodies and result
bindings; they do not establish facts that depend on which path executes.
Immutable value snapshots keep their existing treatment. This restores the
absence proof of LLP 3000.007 §20.5 without changing the device interpreter.
The package README and prediction card describe the rule, and the card
compiles a guarded explicit-mint like alongside its set-state recipe.

The binder regression checks 14 forms. The expanded device agreement test
checks 20 forms on each of two stores (40 cases), with server execution for
every case and predicted application rows equal to the server's where
prediction succeeds. After the repair there are 0 binder/runtime mismatches.
The unrelated require predicts 1 row on each store; a branch or two-iteration
loop assigning the parameter predicts 0. An unrelated insert plus the final
insert predicts 2 rows. Copying a mint alias and assigning another local
preserve the untouched alias's proof. The lesson is that a local's mint fact
is invalidated by a write to that local, not by an arbitrary statement boundary.

## 2026-09-15 — Wave 5 confirmation N3: the lead's fix after the round limit

The GPT confirmation of round 3 (`1688940ff`) found both N1 and N2 repaired,
and reported one new Medium, N3.

**The defect.** Client A submits a write and sees `pending`. Native owner B,
sharing the device store, persists the receipt and marks the shared outbox
entry sent; catch-up then leaves it queued. A's next flush read B's durable
receipt and skipped `emitWrite` because a receipt was already known. A had
never emitted that completion, so a mounted `usePendingWrite` stayed pending.
Grok's confirmation was READY.

**Why the lead fixed it.** The three-round limit had been reached, and the
fix is one line with a regression test, so the lead made it instead of
opening a fourth round. `flushOnce` now always calls `emitWrite` for a sent
queued entry. Emission is tracked per client, and the emitted set (kept while
the outbox entry exists, W5R2a) suppresses a repeat. Re-reading the receipt
still never refreshes an evicted one.

**Regression.** `W5 confirmation N3: another owner's durable receipt still
notifies this client once` (`test/acquisition.test.mjs`, process tier, two
owners): `first_completion_emissions=0` without the fix, `1` with it.
`W5R2a … a sent queued id emits once beyond 256 other emissions` (wasm and
process) and the W5R1x history tests stay green: 15/15 for
`--test-name-pattern='N3|W5R2a|W5R1x'`.

## 2026-09-15 — Wave 6 W6b: password characters and the guest choice

Built against `35886bc2226f8e53b2537132714d6f3e6890f140`, from the 0.2.21
friction review's H1 and V3 / d-01 and d-02. The shared core signup preparation
now counts Unicode scalar values for the eight-character minimum. Its
1,024-byte maximum still runs first, before hashing. Both the direct core
signup and HTTP signup use this preparation; the repository has no built-in
password-change or password-reset API. Login retains its byte bound.
The refusal stays E_AUTH: its wire message changes from
`E_AUTH: a password needs at least 8 UTF-8 bytes` to
`E_AUTH: a password needs at least 8 characters`. The maximum's wire message
remains `E_AUTH: a password is at most 1024 UTF-8 bytes`.

The personas card and package README name Unicode scalar values and explicitly
tell email-and-password products to declare `use identity password`; plain
`use identity` also mints guests. The chat schema has that choice on its
identity line, which `init --expo` embeds. Expo keeps its working guest opener.
Default and online init are persona-only todo templates with both identity
methods disabled, not password-only products, so their defaults stay disabled.
The onboarding paragraph also points password-only products to checking handle
availability after signup with the new session. No optional declared minimum
was added: that would extend the parser and schema beyond this policy repair.

Measured through core signup, production HTTP, and the published SDK helpers:
seven characters at 7 / 14 / 28 UTF-8 bytes refuse; eight at 8 / 16 / 32 bytes
sign up and log in. Two emoji (2 scalars / 8 bytes) refuse. The core also
accepts four decomposed accented letters (8 scalars / 12 bytes), distinguishing
the scalar policy from grapheme counting. The maximum accepts 1,024 ASCII,
512 accented, or 256 emoji scalars at 1,024 bytes and refuses one more ASCII
byte on signup and login. The HTTP and SDK witnesses repeat the 512-scalar
boundary. All three identity forms advertise and enforce their modes: the
password-only form refuses `/auth/guest`, and the other two mint guests.

## 2026-09-15 — W6d: caller-supplied mutation ids (0.2.21 calibration H7)

Base: `35886bc2226f8e53b2537132714d6f3e6890f140`. The online client and the
shared web/native local client now accept `mutate(op, args, { id })`.
The caller id is the outbox and server mutation id, and the id recovered by
`write` and `usePendingWrite`. Prediction still supplies independent row ids
through `new_ids`. No engine replay behavior, serialized value form, meter
ceiling or existing corpus case changed.

The id has the minted 128-bit form: 26 uppercase Crockford base32 digits,
starting with 0–7. Invalid ids return typed local `E_WRITE_ID`; even a
non-string JavaScript input returns a Write-shaped refusal. Arguments are
snapshotted as JSON before admission. Concurrent retries share the admission
and the pending Write object. Known operation/argument mismatches return
`E_WRITE_ID_REUSE` without replacing the original outcome or emitting a false
terminal event. JSON object key order is immaterial.

Settled retries recover the existing value-free receipt (LLP 3000.007 §17).
Input identities are held for unresolved writes and up to 256 terminal writes;
the client keeps id-only markers for its lifetime after that window. A known
id whose receipt and queued entry have gone returns `E_WRITE_RECEIPT_EXPIRED`,
so that client never admits it twice. Reopen can ask the server for the old
outcome. A recovered receipt alone has no input identity to compare; without
local evidence, the server's `(principal, mutation id)` record wins even if
operation or arguments differ. This guarantee belongs to that backend store.
The README, writes card, contract JSDoc and generated api.ts JSDoc state these
boundaries; all three new codes are in `guide::CODES`.

Recovery loads queued and retained ids during open. Fresh admissions still
reach the synchronous web journal before mutate returns its promise
(LLP 3000.007 §20.4); putting an awaited receipt lookup before every admission
would have weakened navigation custody. The journal witness checks a same-id
retry and a conflicting retry cannot overwrite that original record.

Measured against the real HTTP host, with the wasm device and process/native
device as the two local tiers:

- Each of 3 tiers: 1 POST, 1 application, 1 terminal event for ordinary same-id
  retries; a lost acknowledgement causes 2 identical POSTs and 1 application,
  with 0 historical result fields in the replay receipt.
- Each of 2 local tiers after offline reopen: 1 queued entry, 1 predicted row,
  1 POST and 1 application. The predicted row id differs from the write id.
- Each tier: 9 malformed ids refused locally; the maximum 128-bit id succeeds.
  After 257 completed writes, 256 receipts remain, a known-id retry makes 0
  new admissions, and reopening recovers through 1 server POST.
- Synchronous web custody: 1 journal record, 1 durable outbox entry and 1
  application despite concurrent same-id and conflicting-input retries.

Verification used Node 24.18.0. Before implementation, the 11 W6d regressions
reported `ℹ pass 0` / `ℹ fail 11`; afterward, `ℹ pass 11` / `ℹ fail 0`.
The expanded final lane tests report `ℹ pass 15` / `ℹ fail 0`; the separate

## 2026-09-15 — W6e: development clock advances preserve live effect leases

Built the 0.2.21 calibration's V4 and H8 (ranks 8 and 11), from base
`35886bc2226f8e53b2537132714d6f3e6890f140`. This was **not a W5g regression**:
W3d commit `91d4ca9b184ff07de268d7eaae638b6a3b422e4f` moved both effect
claims and lease sweeps from wall time to the development clock. Its journal
entry explicitly lists effect leases among the consumers. W5g commit
`f3e781096799a188a896a21047722a97fdc9f34c` subsequently moved presence grace.
The regression on the unchanged base implementation claimed a 60-second lease,
advanced 120 seconds through the actual clock CLI, observed the effect queued
again, and received E_EFFECT_LEASE on settlement: 0 passed / 1 failed.

Chose the brief's lease-extension option: an explicit development advance
adds exactly its duration to running effects' lease deadlines. It preserves
their remaining real-time lifetime without changing retry `next_at`, ordinary
maintenance ticks, action routes or `serve`. The advance takes the engine lock
before the clock lock, matching claims, and publishes the new clock only after
the lease transaction succeeds; invalid clock input leaves leases untouched.
A lease already overdue stays overdue. The simulator checks two successive
120-second advances, an already expired claim, a still-live claim, untouched
queued retry times, real elapsed expiry and successful subsequent settlements.
No value serialization, meter ceiling, conformance case or production route
changed. The existing RFC's development-clock section records the decision;
the effects card and README explain it, and the jobs card and README warn that
rows stamped under an offset keep their times after restart: use a fresh store
per offset test. Persistent row times and a process-local clock are different
things, which the previous restart wording left too easy to conflate.

`runWorker` now prints a lost effect settlement as information, with the effect
ID and cause, instead of passing an Error to `onError`. Other settlement
refusals still report errors. The success-handler and throwing-handler
regressions first reported 0 passed / 2 failed, then passed in the final worker
suite. For the test effect ID, the previous error text was
`Error: E_EFFECT_LEASE: E_EFFECT_LEASE: effect effect-test is queued and not claimed by this worker; claim it first`;
the new informational line is
`snapback4 worker: effect effect-test lease expired; the effect was requeued`.
The backend's E_EFFECT_LEASE refusal stays unchanged for an actual lost claim.

Measurements (N=1, this loaded host): a **120,000 ms** advance on a host started
with **+90,000,000 ms** offset preserved a **60,000 ms** lease, added exactly
**120,000 ms** to its deadline, requeued **0** effects and settled at attempt
**1**, in **13 ms** wall time. A retry with **4,000 ms** backoff became claimable
at attempt **2** after a **4,000 ms** advance in **7 ms** wall time. Actual
**1,000 ms** lease losses requeued **1** effect each in dev and serve, with
late settlements refused and the second attempts successfully settled; the
ordinary five-second sweep observed them after **5,065 ms** and **5,028 ms**.

Targeted checks, from `snapback4/` with Node 24.18.0 on PATH:
`cargo test -p snapback4 --test clock -- --nocapture` passed **12/12**;
`cargo test -p snapback4-sim --test clique effect -- --nocapture` passed **1/1**;
`cargo test -p snapback4-lang --test guide -- --nocapture` passed **24/24**;
`node --test packages/snapback4/test/worker.test.mjs` passed **12/12**.
The first package build found missing generated wasm bindings; running
`bash scripts/build-wasm.sh` supplied them and the package build passed.
An initial misplaced Cargo invocation at the repository root exited 101 before
the regression ran; the recorded Rust test results all come from `snapback4/`.

`bash snapback4/scripts/test.sh` completed in **338 s**, with **954 passed,
2 failed, 4 ignored** across 61 Rust targets, fixtures **9/9**, and client
**313 passed / 1 failed**. All builds and typechecks passed. The Rust failures
were `driver::cli_preserves_every_existing_output` and
`driver::cli_concurrent_runs_into_one_namespace_have_one_owner`, both in the
witness CLI suite; `cargo test -p snapback4 --test witness cli_ -- --nocapture`
then passed **13/13**, including both. These are observed transient failures,
not a verified pre-existing attribution. The client failure was the brief's
known Chromium sandbox SIGABRT in `react.test.mjs`; rerunning
`node --test packages/snapback4/test/react.test.mjs` reproduced **0 passed /
1 failed**. The lead still needs its outside-sandbox browser run. No unrelated
failure is claimed reproduced against the base commit. Reference validation
passed with 0 errors and 0 unchecked; changed code tops out at **1,448 lines**.
The tree is left uncommitted, with no push, tag or publication.

## 2026-09-15 — W6R1a: recipe binding safety and precise horizon advice

Built review findings A–E from wave-6 base
`3bfef6725f2c12b860a81ec866c8560416f85645`. Governing context: LLP 3000
§6–§7 (the simulator invariants and execution decisions), LLP 3000.007
§6.2 (site-based residency), §18.1 (wide-merge guidance), §20.3 (Following),
and §20.5 (insert proofs), under the author's §14 rulings. No core value
serialization, meter ceiling, existing conformance case, client/caller-id
file or worker changed. No commit, push, tag or publication was made.

Recipe installation now checks the global references that its syntax walker
leaves unrenamed, including builtins, against the app's declarations before
writing. The review's `fn count(value: json <=100000): 0` previously installed
successfully; now it refuses with the declaration and file. Renaming that
helper allows installation and restores the 51st-follower promotion/delivery.
The prefix keeps app `copy` and `deliver` functions separate, proved both by
calling the app helpers and by running recipe delivery beside zero-returning
app helpers. Qualified schedule targets are handled as module and operation
tokens; a declared local operation is renamed, and external targets retain
their spelling. Empty/nonempty prefixes and qualified/unqualified targets
are covered. The relationship-driven `N_WIDE_MERGE` and feeds-card adopt
line now use `snapback4 init --recipe feeds --prefix feed`.

Rule probes into a live aggregate collect its expiring-source dependency,
using the same collector as explicit aggregate reads. This includes the
final `after insert <- exists` constraint: a final-review regression was red
before adding the same dependency there. The source appears in persistent
prediction summaries and suppresses a horizon recommendation that would
remove prediction. Whole-partition suppression now includes only point/exists,
rule/live-aggregate and successful insert-arm sites; an ordinary held page
still gets growing-table advice. On both stores, a live rule predicts with
one fully held source row, queues without a row with a one-row source horizon,
and the server refuses a write after that source expires without a sweep.

For `N_HORIZON_GUARD`, chose to skip application-invariant codes rather than
infer that a row-id check is redundant. Only underscore-delimited `DUPLICATE`,
`RETRY` or `DEDUPE` words trigger the advisory. The text explicitly distinguishes
the argument row id from the mutation write id and still makes removal
conditional on retry-only intent. `EVENT_REMOVED` receives no such note;
its ordinary horizon residency remains visible. README, feeds and prediction
cards explain these decisions. No new diagnostic code was introduced.

The additional wired Following witnesses use the published app-card join
with public, private and horizon-limited app posts, each before and after
celebrity promotion. Both stores return null private cards to a non-author;
the author still reads them. A one-row horizon returns the recent card and
null for the older card with `complete: false`. Foreign tombstone writes refuse on the server without changing the feed,
and the author's ordinary removal succeeds; both-store witnesses read
that same wired schema and server state. The public reference-event metadata remains the
recipe's explicitly public surface; it does not grant access to private
app content.

Measurements: installation checks both prefixes (empty and `feed`); **51**
followers promote the author; **52** pull rows cover the author plus followers;
a subsequent post writes **1** broadcast entry and delivers **1** entry to
follower 51 with **3** examined rows. Wired witnesses return **2** entries,
with **8** examined for pushed delivery and **9** for the broadcast branch,
on both stores. The private reader receives **0** app cards; the author
receives **2**. A **1**-row horizon supplies **1** of the **2** app cards and
reports incomplete. These are deterministic correctness/meter observations,
not latency or competitor claims. The largest changed code file is **1,356**
lines (`snapback4-sim/tests/clique.rs`).

### Diagnostic texts, verbatim

B, before:

```text
schema.q:14:1 — N_WIDE_MERGE: query following: read cost grows with the number of related principals (up to 1001 lanes); a read past the 8,192 examined ceiling returns `complete: false`
  rewrite: keep read-time merges for a bounded small number of related principals; for Following, `snapback4 init --recipe feeds`; measure with `snapback4 test --cost`
  guide: feeds
```

B, after:

```text
schema.q:14:1 — N_WIDE_MERGE: query following: read cost grows with the number of related principals (up to 1001 lanes); a read past the 8,192 examined ceiling returns `complete: false`
  rewrite: keep read-time merges for a bounded small number of related principals; for Following, `snapback4 init --recipe feeds --prefix feed`; measure with `snapback4 test --cost`
  guide: feeds
```

A previously exited 0 with empty stderr. After, for both prefixes:

```text
init: recipe cannot be installed; no files written
  fn count in ./snapback/helpers.q:1:1 would shadow the recipe's unrenamed reference `count` in snapback/feed.q
  rename the app declaration `count` and its callers, then run init again
```

E, before, for an application invariant:

```text
schema.q:7:22 — N_HORIZON_GUARD: act: `require not exists tombstones[eventId] else EVENT_REMOVED` reads an argument id past a horizon; the write id already dedupes retries for this principal, and this guard costs offline prediction on a miss
  rewrite: if this guard only dedupes retries, remove `require not exists tombstones[eventId] else EVENT_REMOVED` and keep the insert; retry with the same mutation write id. A fresh write id is a new write; keep guards that enforce an application requirement
  guide: prediction
```

After: no `N_HORIZON_GUARD` for `EVENT_REMOVED`. A retry condition still
gets the advisory, now with distinct identities:

```text
schema.q:7:22 — N_HORIZON_GUARD: act: `require not exists tombstones[eventId] else DUPLICATE` reads the argument row id `eventId`, not the mutation write id; a miss past the horizon cannot prove row absence, so this call queues without a predicted row
  rewrite: if this guard only dedupes retries, remove `require not exists tombstones[eventId] else DUPLICATE` and keep the insert; retry with the same mutation write id for this principal. That id dedupes the mutation, not the argument row id; a new mutation write id with the same row id is a different write. Keep guards that enforce an application requirement
  guide: prediction
```

C, before, advice that would remove prediction:

```text
schema.q:1:1 — N_NO_HORIZON: table sessions: `sync public` has no horizon, so every row of every group a device holds reaches it and stays; a device that holds many groups, or a public table that grows, pays for all of it at every cold start
  rewrite: sync public last 500 by byExpiry
  guide: sync
```

After: that note is absent, and adding the horizon is visible persistently:

```text
1 mutation eligible, but these reads queue without a row past a horizon: act (sessions by byOwner (insert actions rule)) — snapback4 why <op>
```

The ordinary archive-page control previously had no growing-table note;
after:

```text
schema.q:1:1 — N_NO_HORIZON: table archive: `sync public` has no horizon, so every row of every group a device holds reaches it and stays; a device that holds many groups, or a public table that grows, pays for all of it at every cold start
  rewrite: sync public last 500 by byTime
  guide: sync
```

## 2026-09-15 — W6R1b: caller write ids across owners and receipt eviction

Built the wave-6 round-1 caller-id corrections from
`3bfef6725f2c12b860a81ec866c8560416f85645`. Device admission now compares
operation, JSON arguments and viewer inside the writer transaction before
prediction. Equal input returns the original entry, including its submission
number, timestamp and minted row ids; conflicting input returns
`E_WRITE_ID_REUSE` without a prediction, outbox replacement, receipt or terminal
event. Fresh admissions allocate after the durable submission counter inside
that same transaction. SQLite's existing immediate transaction and the memory
host's serialized calls already provide the required boundary; neither store
implementation needed a change. The two-owner client witness uses two native
processes on one SQLite file, and two already-open native-shaped clients over
one serialized wasm memory device. Separate live web tabs retain their existing
independent stores and are deduplicated at the server.

A caller-supplied id with no local outcome now carries `replay_candidate` in its
synchronous admission request and navigation journal. A prediction or validation
refusal rolls back its savepoint and queues without rows, so the server can
consult its authoritative replay record. This also covers a changed or missing
local operation; the server's replay lookup precedes current-generation shape
validation. An admitted no-row entry needs only its existing `predictable: false`
state; the flag is not a new serialized value or an outbox state. A restore halt
still refuses admission. The request flag required a minimal device dispatcher
change in `call.rs`; `snapback4-core/src/error.rs` gives the already-published
`E_WRITE_ID_REUSE` code its input family, unchanged message and writes guide.
Those are the two supporting production files outside the lane's named files.
No worker, recipe/diagnostics lane, meter ceiling or existing corpus case changed.

The first client regression run was `ℹ tests 17`, `ℹ pass 4`, `ℹ fail 13`;
its fixed run was `ℹ tests 17`, `ℹ pass 17`, `ℹ fail 0`. The direct device
regression first reported
`test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 135 filtered out; finished in 0.11s`
and then
`test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 135 filtered out; finished in 0.11s`.
Adding an overlapping retry on the losing client found another race: it could
collect the winner's pending receipt while the first losing call refused.
`node --test --test-name-pattern=conflicting packages/snapback4/test/write-ids.test.mjs`
went from `ℹ pass 0` / `ℹ fail 4` to `ℹ pass 4` / `ℹ fail 0` after sharing the
admission refusal with overlapping callers. A losing reservation is forgotten
so a later retry can recover the original input. Retrying a known id after
sign-out returns the call's authentication refusal without overwriting the sent
receipt or emitting another terminal event; the closed-client witness also
passes. No `writeIdFor` helper was added: the writes card, README and contract
now say to store a `mintId()` with the intent or fixture; arbitrary fixture
strings still need an application ledger.

Measurements on both device stores: **1 original prediction, 1 durable entry,
1 applied row and 0 conflicting terminal events**, for equal/conflicting input
both offline and during an in-flight send. After **256** other completions evict
an explicit-row or guarded write's receipt, reopen queues **0** predicted rows,
makes **1** recovery POST and receives the original `sent, replayed: true`
receipt, with **0** duplicate rows. A fresh id still receives the server's real
refusal. The previous explicit-row message was
`records already has a row with id R`; the guard message was
`the program refused with LOCKED`. Both retries now report pending with
`queued without a row: local data does not justify prediction` and then replay
success. The reuse message remains
`write id already belongs to a different operation or arguments; retry the original input or use a new id`.
The same id under **2 principals** produces **2 independent applications** and
**2 POSTs**, on online, memory and native clients. **2 live web tabs** capture
**2 synchronous journal records**, send **2 POSTs** and apply **1** write.
Caller-id journal replacement tests send **0** writes, including after offline
recovery; these inject a replacement identity in real sync replies. A separate
lost-admission-save/changed-guard witness retains **1** replay candidate across
reopen and makes **1** replay POST. The wasm build measured **1,752,840 B raw /
488,262 B gzip**, versus base **1,751,309 B / 487,926 B**: **+1,531 B raw /
+336 B gzip**. The largest changed code file is **1,261 lines**.

## 2026-09-15 — W6R1c: truthful lost-effect reports and action claims across clock advances

Base: `3bfef6725f2c12b860a81ec866c8560416f85645`. Reproduced both wave-6
review findings before their fixes. The worker's 10 mocked outcome cases
reported `ℹ pass 0` / `ℹ fail 10`; four real-wire cases reported
`ℹ pass 0` / `ℹ fail 4`. The real wire expired a throwing handler's lease,
exhausted the eighth attempt, let another service settle the effect, and let
another service retain its claim. The action regression reported
`test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 12 filtered out; finished in 1.32s`:
a 120,000 ms advance had swept the live action into `queued`.

`runWorker` now reports the server's code and full message. Only the exact
queued-state refusal is informational and says requeued; sent, running,
failed and unknown outcomes still call `onError` (or the stderr fallback).
Matching the complete refusal avoids an extra listing whose state could
belong to a newer attempt, and unfamiliar wording stays an error. If a
handler threw and settlement is refused or throws, a `finally` reports the
original error object and stack separately. Successful failure settlement
still records the provider error through the ordinary retry path. The final
worker diff keeps the existing handler execution and serialization path.
The 14 lost-lease cases passed after the fix; the complete final worker
suite passed 24/24 in 28,703.581042 ms.

The shared development advance now shifts held action deadlines and their
delegated viewer-session expiries in the same transaction as effect leases.
Its helper is renamed `advance_worker_leases`; the only simulator edits are
the two existing callers. The clock is published only after that transaction
commits. A test-forced failure of its last update leaves the effect deadline,
action deadline, viewer-session expiry and clock unchanged. Invalid advance
input also leaves deadlines unchanged. Ordinary service credentials keep
their expiry; retry timestamps stay put; overdue sessions stay overdue;
settlement still revokes the original action token. Production clock and
expiry paths are unchanged. No meter, serialized value or existing corpus
case changed; no new diagnostic code or language form was added.

Measurements (N=1, this shared host): two 120,000 ms advances extend the held
60,000 ms action lease and viewer session by exactly 240,000 ms, preserve
a concurrently held effect, requeue 0 actions, and settle the original claim
at attempt 1, in 78 ms wall time. A real 1,000 ms action lease expires and is
reclaimed at attempt 2 in both dev and serve (1,012 ms and 1,004 ms observed).
A queued action's 4,000 ms backoff is made due by a 4,000 ms advance with
0 ms change to `next_at`, and attempt 3 settles. The real effect exhaustion
case records `failed` at attempt 8. The largest changed source has 1,456
lines; Markdown is not reflowed to meet a source-file cap.

but the suggested index is now compared with every eligible mutation's
bound scans. An ascending page or a page on another index replaces the

prediction. A descending page on the suggested index keeps the declaration.

module identity and compares qualified schedule targets with that identity.

local. `other.purgeRemoved` stays that target with output module arguments

## 2026-09-15 — two HTTP framing experiments do not justify adoption

The performance lane completed two separate fixed 68b45b9a / 0.2.20 native
Linux A/B experiments. Neither changes the production runtime. Raising the
JSON chunk threshold increased concurrent-stream median p99 from 155.006
to 189.457 ms, with p50/p99/rate losses in all three pairs. Keeping the
original framing but reserving chunk overhead lost median throughput in
seven of eight cases and raised large initial C8 snapshot p99 from 96.254
to 112.928 ms. Its separate fixed-header buffer-growth probe is not an
RSS or peak-memory measurement.

Each experiment passed 9,600 timed requests, 960 excluded warmups, 192
ordinary-auth captures, 48 complete walks and 144 reconstructed page hashes.
All twelve server/client groups per experiment stopped. Both frozen
calculators passed and independent evidence audits retain every loss:
19 median / 55 paired for known-length framing, 29 / 67 for reservation.
Two complete original-evidence records are appended to storage.jsonl; the
[benchmark record](../benchmarks/runs/snapback4-public-catalog-20260913/README.md)
includes every case and the source/host/correctness/timing limits. The
private comparison continues separately; these results establish no new
competitor ranking or moving-main speed claim.


## 2026-09-15 — W7a: installed Following authority, offline prediction and saturated promotion

Built against `80b4899f949eb597d6426d95dda82d0c2dcd0b97` for the 0.2.22
calibration's d-03, H1/H2/H9 and ranks 1/3/8. Used the `llp-orient` context:
LLP 3000 §6–§7 (prediction convergence and the Snapback 4 fence), LLP
3000.007 §6.2/§6.8 (eligibility and measured acquisition), §14 (author
rulings), §18.1 (bounded merge guidance), and §20.3 (Following). The latter
now records the implemented tradeoff. No new LLP or workflow was created.

### What changed

With `--prefix`, the installer converts the recipe's seven standalone
mutations into `fn` helpers through parser-selected declaration lines before
renaming references. Only Following remains a client query; purge is a system
job. Generated `src/following.ts` has no mutation wrappers. The installed
`feedCreatePost` can no longer be called by a client to insert a ghost, and
the app's own create/repost path creates or validates its app post. Unprefixed
standalone reference-event operations remain available. W6R1's binding-safety
witness now explicitly drives prefixed helpers through its test app.

Author modes alone were not enough for prediction: the helpers also read
follows and source events, write synced tables, and used `if absent` on
another reader's private inbox. The recipe now fully syncs public modes,
reference events, graph edges and pull routes, with global metadata caps of
1,000 authors, 60,000 source events, 100,000 edges and 32,000 pull routes.
Existing per-account limits and every engine meter ceiling stay unchanged.
A fresh event or new follow establishes a fresh copy; unconditional copy
inserts avoid a hidden inbox absence proof. Predicting loops cover the
schema cap, and backfill stops after the newest 200 events. The wired card
adds a real `saveProfile` example. Its profile save, post and follow predict
on both stores after acquisition, including a post with another reader's
private delivery. App post visibility remains its own rule, as the existing
public/private/horizon witnesses verify.

Promotion attempts each pull insertion and skips a reader already at 32.
It succeeds with a saturated existing follower and with a saturated author.
A skipped follower keeps pushed history but misses later broadcasts until
freeing a slot and unfollowing/refollowing; `complete` covers installed lanes.
A saturated author's own shared post gets an own-inbox copy. New follows of
already-shared authors refuse `FEED_PULL_CAP` when no slot exists, atomically
rolling back the app edge. The code is explained in `guide::CODES`.
Edges record `at: now`; imported edges default to `0` for unknown age. A
wall-clock import default initially made paired privacy fixtures unequal;
using an explicit historical default preserves their identical public worlds.

Removal now predicts, and a forged tombstone is refused locally as well as
on the server. Its existing tests were updated to settle their predicted
removal receipts before delivering a fresh repost, so an outstanding
`unrepost` does not intentionally replay against that new event. All 901
readers in the large removal scenario still observe removal, purge and
re-repost on both stores. No private inbox is made public.

### Measurements

- Wired fixture: 502 authors, 505 bridged edges (5 and 500 follows), 526 app
  cards including an image, and 2 reposts. `test --residency` measures the
  500-follow reader at **3,095 rows / 335,403 B**, up from 1,055 rows.
  Breakdown: authors 502 / 39,154 B; recipe edges 505 / 50,490 B; source
  references 528 / 63,830 B; inbox 527 / 90,565 B; app edges 505 / 46,955 B;
  app cards 526 / 44,235 B; reposts 2 / 174 B. Other tables are empty.
- The 5-follow reader acquires **2,600 rows**. Both readers return **20/20**,
  complete, with **82 examinations / 21 probes / 0 index entries**, on
  the server and both device stores. Sampled p95 ms (5 / 500): server
  **1.695 / 1.444**, memory **0.841 / 0.826**, SQLite **2.050 / 1.656**.
  These are shared-host observations, not latency assertions.
- The larger existing recipe fixture (1,000 authors, 50,000 events, 1,415
  edges) acquires **78,566 rows** for 500 follows, including **25,050**
  private entries. Its 5-follow reader acquires **53,816 rows**. This
  fixture has no app-card joins. Measurements use real snapshots.
- Offline `saveProfile` / `createPost` / `follow`: **2 / 3 / 3 predicted
  rows** on each store; a post with one follower predicts **4 rows**.
- Promotion: **51 followers**, **1 saturated follower skipped**, that
  reader stays at **32 pulls**, and follower 51 receives the new broadcast.
  A saturated author also stays at **32 pulls** and sees their own post.
- Removal and purge: **901 readers** per store in the 900-follower case;
  the maximal purge body still handles **1,001 copies / 1,002 writes**.
- Largest changed code file: `snapback4-sim/tests/clique.rs`, **1,407**
  newline-terminated lines (`wc -l`), below the 1,500-line cap.

This deliberately pays more public metadata acquisition for synchronous
prediction and complete backfill. It does not reduce cold sync or make it
proportional only to this reader's follows; the card and README publish
both fixture sizes. A deferred delivery/backfill job would make a different
latency tradeoff and was not introduced.
