## 2026-09-15 — W7d: search every chat at 100–1,000 memberships

Lane `sb4/w7d`, base `80b4899f949eb597d6426d95dda82d0c2dcd0b97`.
The search card now carries a complete full-history device form and a
server walk with two independent cursors: discover 50 memberships, exhaust
that batch's matching-result cursor, then advance membership discovery.
The README points to it. N_WIDE_MERGE for matching searches points to this
section, and the code catalog explains why one result cursor cannot
continue undiscovered chats or a meter-cut merge. Group results by chat;
a single globally ordered stream needs every batch's head. The card names
horizons, live membership changes, the 32-word bound and meter cuts.

The new device witness found a real cursor defect before the fix: an eager
word lane validated its shared merge token as a direct cursor scoped to
one word, rejecting page two with `E_INPUT: cursor: cursor token describes
a different prefix or generation`. The minimal core change passes no
direct-prefix scope while validating a generated word lane, matching the
existing lazy lane path. Direct plain-page prefix/generation checks and all
serialized forms remain unchanged. This extra core file was necessary to
make the recommended device walk work. LLP 3000.007 §18.1 records it.

The fixture is the card's actual Quarry, extracted by the shared test
helper. It has 30 messages per held chat: 24 coffee hits and 6 tea misses,
a single first-term word prefix, tied timestamps across chats, and one
unreadable chat containing newer hits. Device tests acquire, close and
reopen both SQLite and memory stores. Every expected id appears once and
results group into every expected chat; the unreadable chat stays absent.

| 500 | 12,000 / 500 | 15,000 | 22 / 13,198 | 1,201 / 396,149 |

A ten-message acquisition horizon instead acquires 1,000 / 5,000 / 10,000

The unbatched 1,000-lane alternative examines 2,400 / 8,358 / 8,880 on the

The optional maintained per-reader inbox was investigated by copy cost and

## 2026-09-15 — W7b: grace defers a push instead of swallowing it

Built calibration 0.2.22 d-02 / V2 from base
`80b4899f949eb597d6426d95dda82d0c2dcd0b97`. Before changing the engine, the
real-HTTP regression sent a message after an ended poll and found an empty
effect queue: `test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 14 filtered out; finished in 1.14s`.
After the fix, that same command reported
`test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 14 filtered out; finished in 1.42s`.

The states are recorded in LLP 3000.007 §19.1. A live poll still suppresses
an absence-conditioned push. No live poll and no grace emits immediately.
For a mutation whose presence values reach only effects, grace alone now
means a deferred absence decision, with the effect's existing `next_at` at
the grace deadline. Dependencies follow local values, fields and branch
control, including lowered short-circuit expressions, and stay separate for
each recipient; an unrelated emit stays immediate. The binder's existing
effects-only proof keeps predicted rows independent of this server decision.
Ordinary presence queries, and presence deciding rows or results, retain
their prior meaning. No serialized value/IR form or meter ceiling changed.

An authenticated reconnect during the waiting window is recorded durably
with the queued effect, under the same engine lock as emission and claim.
At first claim, that record or a currently live poll cancels worker delivery:
state `satisfied`, result `{ outcome: 'presence_reconnected' }`, attempts `0`.
This survives a brief reconnect followed by disconnect and restart. An ended
reconnect after the window does not cancel it. The first actual claim consumes
the presence condition; subsequent retries keep the existing worker protocol.
The queue and reconnect records share the mutation's transaction; replay and
restart cannot create a second effect. Development deadlines follow the dev
clock, while `serve` converts its remaining monotone grace into the queue's
wall-clock deadline. The process-local dev offset still resets on restart.

Measurements (local loaded host): a `36,000 ms` CLI advance made a push with
`35,000 ms` remaining delay claimable in `5 ms` wall time in the targeted HTTP
run: `1` delivered effect, `1` attempt, `0` duplicate claims. The deterministic
boundary test waits `25,000 ms` from message to deadline, claims `0` at
`35,999`, and `1` at `36,000`. Restart cases perform `2` reopens each; absence
and a late-ended reconnect deliver `1`, while an in-window reconnect and a
live poll at claim deliver `0`. The Clique send writes `1` message for `2`
recipients: Bob's reconnect satisfies `1` push and Carol receives `1`.
Both device stores predict `1` row identical to the server's row with `1`
deferred effect. The release-host witness delivers `1` immediate effect,
then persists and satisfies `1` grace effect with `0` worker attempts after
reopen. Its claim clock is pinned in the engine at the persisted deadline;
production exposes no clock-control route.

Final focused checks: grace simulator `6 passed / 0 failed`; presence device
suite `8 passed / 0 failed`; HTTP grace suite `3 passed / 0 failed`; compiled
guide/README suite `25 passed / 0 failed`. The full
`bash snapback4/scripts/test.sh` finished with `== 1 failure(s) in 506 s`:
Rust totals `1,000 passed / 0 failed / 4 ignored` (62 summary lines), fixtures
`9 passed / 0 failed`, clients `364 passed / 1 failed`. Builds and package,
chat and Expo typechecks passed. The client failure is the brief's named
sandbox artifact: Chromium exits `SIGABRT` in `react.test.mjs`; rerunning
`node --test packages/snapback4/test/react.test.mjs` alone gives
`ℹ tests 1` / `ℹ pass 0` / `ℹ fail 1` with the same abort. I did not rerun
that failure against the base, so this is an environment observation, not a
newly verified pre-existing product-failure claim. `./ref-check --verbose`
passes. No commit, push, tag or publication was made.

What I learned: neither a process-local last-seen time nor a claim-time check
alone can remember a reconnect that has already ended. The reconnect fact
must be durable until first claim, alongside the deferred effect. No new
presence table in the application or worker-side timer is needed.
The transaction wording above refers to the initial grace dependency records:
they are inserted with the emitted queue row in the mutation's commit. A later
reconnect marks those records in its own transaction, serialized by the engine
lock; claim consumes them atomically with its final queue transition.

## 2026-09-15 — W7R1a: grace cannot buy a refusal; only necessary absence cancels

Wave-7 review round 1, base
`2cbe3f94bd22d6a9ebbb17c84f6f4e832fd7df2b`. F1 reproduced before the fix:
the same note mutation needed **653 heap bytes without grace**, **1,194 with
grace**. At ceiling 653 the former committed and the latter refused E_BOUND;
the device predicted the note on both stores. The server regression initially
reported `test result: FAILED. 1 passed; 2 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 68 filtered out; finished in 0.06s`;
the device regression reported `test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 145 filtered out; finished in 0.11s`.
After adding the payload/guard deadline case, I temporarily restored the four
core implementation files from the exact base (without switching branches),
ran all four new simulator tests, and restored the intended changes:
`test result: FAILED. 1 passed; 3 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 68 filtered out; finished in 0.07s`.

Every eligible presence read now records a potential dependency, including on
the device and when there is no grace. An optional deadline separates the
reservation from durable grace. Copies through variables, guards and emits
remain charged; propagation avoids an intermediate map copy, and append and
saved dependency slots pay their own allocation allowance; a discarded device emission also pays its copy. Prediction
restores dependency locals and pending reads around the untaken arm. Only
present deadlines are written to `_effect_presence`; the existing stored
forms and ceilings stay the same. The static guard proof is also metered
before executing the mutation, identically on both hosts.

F2 reproduced as an unconditional audit payload becoming `satisfied` with
zero attempts after reconnect. A payload read also incorrectly moved a guard's
20,000 deadline to its own 36,000 deadline. The fix proves necessary absence
before retaining cancellation deadlines. It understands count/zero tests,
boolean aliases, conjunctions and the compiler's short-circuit setup; unknown
forms keep ordinary emission semantics. It does not re-execute application
conditions or writes at claim. The direct and aliased `or force` cases did
not reproduce cancellation on this base, and remain explicit regressions.

This corrects the broader dependency wording in the earlier W7b entry:
**dependency tracking alone never authorizes cancellation**. Payload reads
add no delay and no cancellation condition. An enclosing necessary absence
guard still applies. Conjunctive or nested necessary absence guards wait for
their latest deadline; a reconnect inside any one necessary principal's own
window can satisfy the effect. Alternative guards such as `not online or
force` and `not (online and force)` retain ordinary immediate emission. The
README and presence/effects cards now state that distinction. An existing
negated-conjunction test was updated to require immediate delivery, while its
necessary-conjunction alias case still requires cancellation.

Final deterministic measurements: the simulator note fixture needs **2,018
heap bytes** in both grace worlds, refuses identically at **2,017**, and commits
one note in each at **2,018**. The equivalent `probe` fixture on both device
stores and server needs **2,027**, fails prediction/commit at **2,026**, and
predicts/commits at **2,027**. The fixtures use different operation names. Two-dependency tests use deadlines **20,000** and
**36,000**: Bob reconnecting at **19,999** cancels, Bob at **20,001** does not,
and Carol at **25,000** cancels; claim at **35,999** returns zero. A payload-only
Carol dependency neither moves Bob's **20,000** deadline nor satisfies it.
Correct cancellation retains **0 attempts**; an admitted effect has **1**.

The end-to-end `dev --replay`/`runWorker`/`doctor` witness commits **1 note**,
counts **1 suppressed effect**, invokes **0 handlers**, and records **0
dependency rows** before and after a **36,000 ms** advance. Its normal-dev
control starts with **1 dependency row**, then invokes **1 handler** and
consumes the row. The non-uniform read witness has **0 examined** when absent
and **1 examined** when hidden in opt-in dev counters. Both have **0 heapBytes,
0 indexEntries, 12 outputBytes, 0 probes, 0 rowsWritten, 2 steps**. The exact
production responses are identical and have no meter, as do the ordinary dev
responses. Both worlds use the same authenticated principal and commit count.

## 2026-09-15 — W7R1b: reader-private pull routes and exact search walks

Base: `2cbe3f94bd22d6a9ebbb17c84f6f4e832fd7df2b`. The F3 review brief
supersedes W7a's public-routing choice. `pulls` again reads and syncs only
to its reader. The installed recipe comes from this card, so both prefixed
and standalone installs get the same audience; no installer fork was needed.
The README and generated client example state the prediction boundary.

Atomic promotion still needs to know whether another reader has 32 routes.
The recipe now keeps one online-only `pullCounts` row per reader, capped at
32,000 rows like the global route population. Its **count is public**;
its author IDs are not present, and the table syncs zero rows. This is an
explicit aggregate disclosure, not a claim that routing was already public.
The helpers increment/decrement it in the route's transaction. Raw fixture
imports include matching counts; application adoption uses the helpers.
Foreign route inserts occur only on the author's first promotion; an own
route can be checked directly. No foreign route lookup is used to infer
absence. The counter's global cap includes the author plus 1,000 followers.

`saveProfile` and `createPost` remain eligible: the two-person witness
predicts 2 and 3 rows on both stores; a post with one follower predicts 4.
`follow` and `unfollow` are `predicts: never` and queue without rows because
slot accounting is online-only, including calls that would not promote.
The device witness uses durable admission, then settles and applies the
server commit; Following converges to both expected posts. The CLI's
residency assertion was updated by one line in `crates/snapback4/tests/init.rs`,
the only file outside the lane's named ownership beyond the explicitly
required README and journal. No presence, effects or worker file changed.

The new saturation scenario runs on memory and SQLite: 51 followers,
2 skipped routes (the saturated reader and author), 32 reader routes,
2 posts after freeing a slot and refollowing, 0 duplicates. The saturated
author retains its new post through an own-inbox copy. A refused new follow
rolls back both app and recipe edges; `FEED_PULL_CAP` still says
`the program refused with FEED_PULL_CAP`. Slot counts equal installed routes
after recovery. Count rows never appear in acquisition. The audience witness
checks positive own routes and zero foreign routes through cold acquisition,
a streamed insert and reopen, including an unrelated account.

Measured cold acquisition, from actual snapshots on both stores:

| Shape | Follows | Rows | JSON payload bytes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Wired app | 5 | 2,600 | 250,482 |
| Wired app | 500 | 3,095 | 335,403 |
| 50,000-event recipe | 5 | 52,915 | not measured |
| 50,000-event recipe | 500 | 77,665 | not measured |
| 50,000-event recipe, celebrity plus four | 5 | 52,866 | not measured |

The wired counts apply to both the predicting writes and queued follows on
the same acquired shape; neither wired reader has a pull route. The larger
dense reader previously acquired 78,566 rows with public routing: 901 foreign
routes no longer arrive. Its private inbox remains 25,050 rows. The larger
five-follow reader has 0 pulls; the celebrity-plus-four reader has 1.
Wired Following remains 20 complete entries, 82 examinations and 21 probes.
No meter ceiling, serialized value form or existing corpus case changed.

The search fixture now checks the exact expected ID set and complete ID
sequence, including boundaries between pages. The server resets the ordering
boundary only when it advances to a new membership batch. Crafted cursors
cover positions below and above the lane range and at an actual hidden row's
ordering key (inside the visible timestamp range), plus eight malformed
descriptors/encodings. Four device query shapes on each store exercise 24
valid walks and 64 refusals; three server shapes exercise 9 valid walks and
24 refusals. These added cursor cases passed without an engine change.
Full device holdings yield 2,400 / 12,000 / 24,000 exact hits at
100 / 500 / 1,000 memberships, in 120 / 600 / 1,200 pages. Horizon-10
holdings yield 400 / 2,000 / 4,000 hits and remain incomplete. Server batches
walk all hits in 120 / 600 / 1,200 pages, with maximum examined 1,201;
device pages have maximum examined 22. Hidden chat IDs never appear.

What I learned: a reader audience applies to server mutation reads too.
Changing only the rule made promotion treat foreign routes as absent and
attempt a 33rd route; the new saturation test caught that refusal. Keeping
exact installed routes private therefore needs explicit server accounting
and a documented prediction cost. A public follow edge is not proof that
its broadcast lane was installed. Count-only test assertions also miss ID
substitution and incorrect ordering between pages; the fixture now tests both.

## 2026-09-15 — W7R2: departed Following readers release accounting capacity

Base: `198b1e6e8c50aec03be4bc368d8a16e5061985a5` (wave-7 integration,
round-1 repairs included). N1 was reproducible before changing the recipe:
unfollowing the final shared author left a `pullCounts` row with `used: 0`.
The global count-row cap then represented every past reader, not the readers
with an installed route.

The feeds card and its README copy now give count deletion to
`.readerId = viewer`. `dropFollow` deletes the count row when `used = 1`,
and decrements it otherwise, in the same transaction as the route and edge
removal. Routing remains reader-private, count disclosure remains online-only,
and follow/unfollow still queue without predicted rows. The existing recipe
installer reads this card, so neither `recipe.rs` nor the init implementation
needed a change. No meter, serialized value, corpus case or other lane's
implementation changed.

The shared regression fixture occupies the actual 32,000 route and count-row
caps with real routes and matching counts, not seeded zero rows. It uses 33
shared authors and spreads 31,998 background readers below the per-author
1,000-follower cap, alongside the departing reader and one author's self-route.
As in the existing scale fixture, bulk seed loading temporarily omits schema
caps, then adopts the original schema and validates every cap before the test
operations. Runtime ceilings are unchanged.

On the server and both device stores, count occupancy is
**32,000 → 31,999 → 32,000 → 31,999 → 32,000**: the departing reader leaves,
a new reader follows and leaves, and the first reader re-follows. All four
writes succeed after the fix, each writing **3 rows**. The smaller lifecycle
has **2 → 1 → 0 → 0 → 1** reader routes: the first unfollow keeps the count
row at 1, the second deletes it, a repeated unfollow writes **0 rows**, and
re-follow recreates it. The author's self-route/count stays at **1**.
A separate authority test refuses another reader's deletion and admits the
owner's. The device witnesses durably admit the writes with **0 predicted
rows**, settle against the server, apply its stream, compare complete feeds,
and reopen each store. Count rows and foreign route rows acquired: **0**.

I checked the other Following accounting/scratch state. `removedEvents` is
bounded pending work: `purgeRemoved` deletes every remaining private copy
(up to 1,001) and the tombstone in the same chunk transaction. Existing
server and both-store removal tests pass in the full suite, including
re-removal/re-repost and empty tombstones after cleanup. A parked chunk can
retain its work, as documented; successful cleanup does not strand its slot.
There is no separate recipe purge-state table. The engine's schedule updates
two metadata keys in place; a completed Quarry job clears its cursor/upper
keys. `_jobs` retains completed run history without pruning, so that generic
history can grow, but it has no recipe row cap and cannot consume a Following
routing/tombstone slot. Engine history retention is outside this lane and was
not changed. What I learned: a bounded accounting table needs its own deletion
lifecycle even when the data it counts already has one; an author cap does
not bound unregistered readers over time.

## 2026-09-15 — Postgres evaluation backend (Codex)

Author scope: "Build the evaluation prototype" — real Quarry queries and
mutations, transactional sync records, and measurements before full
CLI/deployment support. Built in the isolated `sb4/postgres-evaluation-20260915`
lane from `35886bc22`; no production backend switch or package publication.

Added opt-in `snapback4-core/postgres`, with the same `Runner` over Postgres
canonical row images and ordered binary index keys. Extracted `PartitionRows`
so both databases use the existing snapshot/stream authorization machinery.
Rows, indexes, maintains, commit head, sync log, effect records and operation
receipts commit atomically. Refused programs keep only their sanitized receipt;
late database failures roll back everything. Read transactions use
repeatable-read. Serialized writes reserve the head; serializable writes retry
the complete operation, with a bound and backoff. The head is transactional,
not a Postgres sequence whose allocation can overtake an earlier commit.

`experiments/postgres` is an independent, unpublished Cargo harness with a
compiled Quarry fixture, PostgreSQL/SQLite comparisons and the existing device.
`bash scripts/test-postgres.sh` starts/stops a private socket-only cluster when
no connection is supplied and retains its data for inspection. Ten tests pass:
ordinary fixture conformance, atomic failure/replay, concurrent writes and
refused-op races, matching rows/watermarks during concurrent commits, membership
snapshot/stream paging, and a real device's offline prediction, persisted queue,
reopen, lost-response retry, settlement and revocation. The tenth-test count
includes a deliberate non-portability witness: 6,000-byte incompressible indexed
text succeeds in SQLite but exceeds the generic Postgres B-tree tuple limit.
It rolls back atomically; this is a documented limitation, not a supported case.

Apple M5, 32 GiB, macOS 26.6.2; PostgreSQL 16.14 and bundled SQLite 3.53.2.
Two recorded release runs (200 and 1,000 timed operations), 32 rooms × 25 items.
The larger run: the Quarry inbox is 0.138 ms median in SQLite, 1.894 ms in
Postgres, with 68 explicit database calls. A separately seeded native relational
join returns the same fixture values in 0.082 ms, without general Snapback
rules/meter/completeness. It is a planning lower bound, not an optimized
Snapback query or a competitor comparison. Four disjoint Postgres writers:
2,624 ops/s serialized, 2,182 serializable, 984 retries for 2,000 commits in the
latter. There are no lost increments. SQLite WAL/FULL and Postgres's normal
durability settings were enabled; these are not identical power-loss guarantees,
and the local microbenchmark is not controlled sustained-load qualification.

Interpretation: keep the application semantics shared, but evaluate batched/
plan-oriented execution and an alternative commit-order design before
productizing this adapter. Full deploy, auth hosting, migration/restore,
external SQL writes, native modules, asset ledger, jobs/actions and effect
workers remain out of scope. No wire or client contract change, no new LLP
number, no new default gate. The temporary feature-level dependency on SQLite
for shared server types is explicit. Full recipe, raw data and limitations:
[`experiments/postgres/README.md`](./experiments/postgres/README.md).

Verification: Postgres evaluation 10/10; core tests with the `postgres` feature;
default core/device suites; complete language suite after the fresh worktree's
`bun install --frozen-lockfile`; simulator library plus membership, maintains
and review-corrections suites; core without default features; harness clippy;
`ref-check --verbose` (0 errors, 0 unchecked). The initial language run stopped
at its explicit missing-Bun-dependencies precondition, then passed after install.
No browser, iOS, full CLI/deployment suite or production publication claimed.

## 2026-09-15 — Draft general-purpose backend architecture (Codex)

## 2026-09-15 — LLP 3000.009 rewritten after a directional review (Claude)

The author asked for a sanity check of Draft 3000.009's direction, and a

experiment's store and measurements, LLP 3000.007 §3, §7, §9 and §10.3, LLP
3000.008 and .008.004, the actions card, and the online client's table-level

transactions; no SQL writes into managed tables; one commit order; durable
work without exactly-once; webhook admission before acknowledgement; restore
as a new store incarnation; LLP 3000.003's verification obligations.

Changed:

- Execution. The draft lowered data fragments to per-backend plans qualified
  against the interpreter. The rewrite keeps the interpreter as the only
  executor and batches access with transaction-scoped prefetch. The inbox's
  68 calls are a per-row loop after a one-call page scan; the meter's charges
  and cut are defined in interpreter order; Convex's Postgres persistence is
  a generic documents-and-indexes layout beneath its own engine.

  engine-maintained projections, which SQL reads (candidates or declared
  channels) and extensions use. If the author admits SQL reads, this answers
  two of the costs LLP 3000.007 §9.1 named.
- Sequence. An online-only brief with Convex and Supabase controls first,
  rerun after each increment, with Postgres as a parallel lane; the draft put
  the application last.
- Terms. "Native" keeps LLP 3000.005's meaning; the draft's native
  capabilities are database capabilities.
- Added: read-set invalidation for online observation, with key ranges kept
  on the server (§7.1).

LLP 3000.003's routing link now names the verification section's new number
(§11), and the root's 3000.009 entry summarizes the rewrite. Documentation
checks: `./ref-check --verbose` ok (481 LLP documents, 0 errors, 0
unchecked); `git diff --check` clean. The RFC is 708 lines and the root
1,202. No runtime source, tests, independent review or publication.

## 2026-09-15 — LLP 3000.009: the panel, its disposition, and the landing (Claude)

Panel, one round, blind, on `187d98b1f`: Astra (`gpt-6-astra`, max, Codex CLI,
read-only sandbox), Grok (`grok-4.6`, xhigh, terminal/edit/write tools denied,
file reads only) and Muse (`muse-spark-1.3`, xhigh, read-only workspace). All
three returned SOUND WITH MAJOR ISSUES, and none proposed another
architecture. The reviews, with their prompt and artifact digests, are
`llp/reviews/3000.009-general-purpose-backend.{gpt,grok,muse}.md`; the
disposition is LLP 3000.009 §15.

The lead checked the load-bearing claims against main before accepting them.
Confirmed: `claim_actions` mints a session from the stored principal
(`engine/actions.rs:131`) while `revoke_principal` deletes only `_sessions`
rows (`identity.rs:459`), so queued work outlives revocation; action replay
compares principal and action, not arguments (`engine/actions.rs:101`); server
mutation replay reads `_ops` by principal and id alone (`store.rs:240`). Two
read-only code maps (the server half; the interpreter's read path and the
Postgres adapter) cut the lanes and decomposed the inbox's 68 calls: BEGIN,
the sequence read, the page scan, 32 maintained-total lookups, 32 rule-probe
lookups, ROLLBACK.

What changed in the RFC: prefetch is a physical cache of exact `Rows` calls,
filled under a savepoint from total keys, charging nothing, qualified by an
on/off differential on Postgres; program-time write batching splits out as C2
and only the commit tail is pipelined in C1; index keys get one portable
bound, and no prefix-and-hash representation without an order proof; authority
is bound at admission, ids are bound to operation and argument digests, and
`ctx.step` records external steps; routes gain a settlement contract, declared
secrets and an explicit worker environment; SQL reads see only authorized
inputs, channels are marked and ship last, liveness follows the whole
dependency set, and expiry uses the operation's clock; increment C splits into
C1–C3 behind one owner for durable non-row state; a Postgres database per
application store is the managed-service assumption. Declined: removing
declared channels outright; moving scheduled actions out of A. `NOT-DOING.md`
gains Moves lines for A1–A3 and C1, and "a jobs framework" narrows.

Landing: the Postgres evaluation and the LLP commits were cherry-picked onto
`bae8b9299` as `sb4/w9-land`. The only conflict was the journal's
append-append, resolved by keeping both sides in order. The evaluation
harness is its own Cargo workspace, so its lockfile needed regenerating
against the core's current dependencies before `--locked` would pass.

Verification on the landing branch: `cargo build`, the wasm build, package
typecheck and build, the chat check, `cargo test --workspace` (910 s), both
app typechecks and the fixture wrapper tests are green; `scripts/test-postgres.sh`
is 10/10 green after the lockfile refresh; `./ref-check --verbose` passes (481

`client tests` step is red, with an ECONNREFUSED cluster against fixture dev

`issues/20260915-snapback4-navigation-model-fixture-server-econnrefused-under-load.md`.
Fix-forward, not a landing veto
(LLP 3000 §4, optimistic landing).

## 2026-09-16 — W8c: adoption health, visible grace deadlines, default dev meters

Lane W8c implements the 0.2.23 friction review's ranks 4, 5 and 8 from
base `78fe08b6468191d2ac0bbe0aa8b9ca3202a493c0`. A writer lock at startup
now keeps startup retrying, with an explicit statement that requests, jobs
and sweeps have not started. A failed watched adoption stays pending without
requiring another save, repeats its reason and consequence on the first
failing background operation, and reopens an obsolete engine through the

## 2026-09-15 — W8a: a cut read says why; held queries stay on the device

Built the 0.2.23 calibration's d-01/d-03 answer on base
`78fe08b6468191d2ac0bbe0aa8b9ca3202a493c0`. Every ready read now carries
`cut: 'meter' | 'words' | null` beside `complete`, from the server and both
device stores through the online, native and web clients. Generated query
comments name the field and the shared `Read` type requires it. React's
paginated read preserves cuts from earlier pages; a meter cut takes precedence
if both kinds occur. Cut sites and counters do not enter the production wire.
No ceiling, row selection, ordering, cursor, value serialization or existing
corpus case changed.

The calibration-shaped simulator fixture seeds exactly 99,090 messages that
match `coffee`, with 44,100 newer unreadable messages ahead of the reader's
first visible row. The unchanged 8,192 examined ceiling records 8,193 charges
including the refused charge: zero rows, incomplete, no cursor. A scoped query
returns 10 readable rows and a complete page. The wire fields, with unchanged
metadata omitted, were `{"data":[],"complete":false,"next":null}` and are now
`{"data":[],"complete":false,"cut":"meter","next":null}`. Separate 33-word
fixtures return nonempty pages with `cut: "words"`; ordinary complete and
complete-empty pages carry `cut: null`. A non-uniform empty server read and a
horizon-limited empty device search remain incomplete with `cut: null`.

`query name(..) held:` declares a device-only query. The compiler records the
marker in execution facts and the generated API, and ordinary `check` explains
`runs: device (held; server refuses E_QUERY_HELD; no server fallback)`.
`dev`, `serve` and `run` refuse before a server scan; for query `heldValue` the
message is `query heldValue is held: it runs only on the device`, and the
rewrite is:

```text
call this query with the local client; for server search, use the scoped server walk in `snapback4 guide search`, section "Search every chat I'm in"
```

The refusal's guide is `search`. The local clients keep held reads local even
when online, cut, or past a horizon. The marker does not acquire data or promise
completeness. The search recipe and language card now demonstrate it; the
recipe loses its irrelevant server N_NEVER_COMPLETE note and keeps its existing
explicit N_NO_HORIZON teaching note.

Regression evidence: before implementation, both the simulator's two tests and
the two-store device suite's two tests were 0 passed / 2 failed (missing cut
and rejected held syntax); afterward each is 2 passed / 0 failed. Seven client
cases cover all three tiers, actual HTTP cut fields, both server modes, held
cuts online/offline, and horizon watches without fallback: 7 passed / 0 failed.
The language/README guide tests are 27 passed / 0 failed, the held `check` test
1 passed / 0 failed, and README TypeScript tests 3 passed / 0 failed.

What I learned: a configured acquisition horizon keeps word search incomplete
even if the current fixture fits under its bound. The reason field must remain
independent of `complete`, and a device-only marker must also stop automatic
server fallback. The contract change exposed one more answer boundary in
React's page aggregation, which now preserves the reason. The reads card was
moved intact into `guide/reads.rs` before adding prose to keep `guide.rs` under
the source-file cap. The Postgres evaluation adapter receives the same outcome
field and held refusal so its optional build retains the shared contract.

## 2026-09-15 — W8R1a: withhold non-uniform server cuts; reserve point-read authorization

Built against `cb98c5de36563f74867a0ef3cbab8de002200616`. The disclosure
rule, verbatim from the reads card:

> Device reads and uniform server reads keep precise reasons.
> Non-uniform server reads report `cut: null`: the reason is withheld, with `complete: false` still truthful.

The card and README say that null means "not disclosed here", not "not cut",
and tell a client to render "Results may be incomplete" for an incomplete
answer with no disclosed reason, including an empty answer. The held-query
recipe and E_QUERY_HELD remain the paved device answer. Development retains
the precise reason in `Read.meter.cut`, with meter taking precedence over
words; the production `serve` response still omits the entire meter object.
The only production change outside the lane's named engine/client files is
that two-line extension of `serve.rs`'s existing dev-only meter encoder.

A point lookup now reserves its rule's static probe allowance before knowing
whether the row is readable, hidden or absent, and evaluates the rule under
that reservation. A short-circuited false verdict pays the same allowance as
a miss. An unpaid allowance remains a cut instead of being mistaken for a
false verdict and erased by meter rollback. Trusted held rows and the system
still need no authorization probes. No meter ceiling, serialized value form,
existing corpus case or CLI/operational implementation changed.

The regression with 4,096 successful two-probe point reads formerly returned
null, complete, uncut, with 8,192 probes. It now returns null, incomplete,
`cut: "meter"`, with 4,096 examinations and 8,194 probes (including the
refused two-probe reservation). With 4,095 prior reads the final visible row
is returned at 8,192 probes without a cut. All three hosts pass 135 paired
hidden/absent point cases across examined and probe boundaries, comparing
all response fields and all seven meter counters.

The original N1 server sweep now includes cut and viewer: 656 identical
hidden/absent pairs over four forms and examined ceilings 1–82. Each device
store runs those 656 pairs on real server-delivered partitions and 164
additional adversarial point-probe pairs on injected online-only rows. The
old artificial hidden device scans are not production partition worlds:
precise device cuts intentionally describe the data a device already holds.
Separate search/point sweeps cover 32 and 33 hidden matching words at seven
examined and seven probe boundaries: 196 full-response pairs per host,
with three positive visible controls per host. Both device stores compare
their wire's coverage fields as well. Actual HTTP `serve` and `dev` each
compare three complete production responses, at 32 words, 33 words and
8,193 hidden rows, with equal commit counts and the same principal. Dev's
private reason remains words or meter where production's cut is null.

Merged pages are covered with meter alone, words alone, and both together;
all withhold next. The 33-word fixture charges 37 examinations; with the
examined ceiling reduced to 10 it still records both cuts and meter wins.
Remembered server meter/word cuts survive disconnection on the online,
process-device and wasm clients. React's existing hook witness now checks
both page orders, plus withheld reasons. The 99,090-message calibration still
examines 8,193 rows past 44,100 hidden rows before finding any visible match;
its public cut is now null, and scoped reads keep their precise reasons.

Red before the fixes: the simulator read-cut group reported `1 passed; 2
failed`, the two device point cases `0 passed; 2 failed`, and the original
N1 server sweep with cut included `0 passed; 1 failed`. Green afterward:
simulator read cuts `4 passed; 0 failed`, device read cuts `6 passed; 0
failed`, N1 server `1 passed; 0 failed`, N1 devices `2 passed; 0 failed`,
compiled guide/README `27 passed; 0 failed`, and the targeted HTTP/client
cases `14 passed; 0 failed`. The lesson is that withholding positions is
not enough: even a reason bit can count hidden work, while rolling back a
failed authorization computation can erase a real limit. Reserve the work
independently of the verdict and disclose only where the workload is public.

Full validation used Node 24.18.0. `bash snapback4/scripts/test.sh` reports
`== 1 failure(s) in 522 s`. Its 62 Rust summaries total 1,054 passed,
zero failed and four ignored; all builds and package/chat/Expo typechecks
pass; fixtures report 9 passed / 0 failed; clients report 382 passed /
1 failed. The sole failure is Chromium SIGABRT during startup in the React
witness, before the hook assertions execute. An isolated rerun with
`node --test packages/snapback4/test/react.test.mjs` again reports 0 passed /
1 failed with that signal. This is the environment artifact named in the
lane brief, not a claim of a green React run or a base-commit verification
of a pre-existing failure; the lead must run the added precedence assertions
outside the sandbox. `./ref-check --verbose` reports 481 LLP docs, 8,982
references, zero errors and zero unchecked. `git diff --check` is clean;

## 2026-09-16 — W9c: bounded emit-only lists and named unique refusals

Base: `ce6cdccebafa0f5fea4fdadf997de1b1e0efb782` (`sb4/w9c`). This lane answers
ranks 7 and 8 and d-05 of the 0.2.24 Clique friction review, including the
0.2.19/0.2.22/0.2.23 recipient-list recurrences and 0.2.23's d-06.

A bounded list loop may now read, compute and emit without preserving one
complete page. The shared admission check still examines row writes in
nested loops, branches and inlined helpers, including helpers inside an
expression. Row-writing populations keep their existing refusal and rewrite.
Every mutation page still passes the uniform/plain-prefix/no-expiry checks;
no ceiling or value encoding changed, and no existing corpus case changed.

`unique byHandle: handle else HANDLE_TAKEN` supplies the code, with the
same default message as `require`. An optional literal supplies an author's
message: `unique byHandle: handle else HANDLE_TAKEN 'That handle is taken.'`.
The original constraint text is retained in `Refusal.detail`, on the server
and both device stores. Hidden collisions still take the existing authority
refusal before this hook; `insert … if absent` still returns null for a visible
clash. The hook is logical schema metadata, so changing wording does not
change the physical index definition. The language card exercises both
code-only and custom-message forms, and runs the duplicate-profile case.
The types, indexes, programs and refusals cards and package README agree.

There is no unknown-code registry in Quarry: `require … else CODE` accepts
any UPPER_SNAKE application code outside `E_`. This lane reuses that exact
validator for unique hooks rather than inventing declarations or rejecting
otherwise valid undeclared codes. The malformed and reserved-code tests
compare against `require`, and CLI `check` rejects both. This is the brief's
one qualification: an unknown-code lookup was not added because no such
lookup exists elsewhere. The optional literal message was the stated
assumption after the clarification received no response.

Measured on six shapes (principal column, int column, alias, filtered page,
shaped page and helper-returned list): **18 executions across 3 hosts**,
**13 authoritative emissions per host** (2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2), **0 application
rows written**, and **0 extra emissions on server replay**. Devices predict
successfully and the subsequent authoritative execution records the effects;
prediction does not deliver effects, as before. Five nested/direct row-write
shapes still refuse. Three uniqueness modes (custom message, code only,
no hook) have positive distinct-handle and negative duplicate-insert cases
on all three hosts. Server tests also cover update collision, `if absent`,
hidden collision and schema serialization. The wasm build measured
**1,797,515 B raw / 499,082 B gzip**; no baseline size comparison is claimed.
The largest changed code file is **1,487 lines**.

## 2026-09-16 — W9R1a: receipt detail and provable held-source coverage

Base: `663cfd6226b7719ed19f98fe7d5e9599ca47a45e`. Implemented the two
wave-9 review findings in the assigned lane. Orientation followed
LLP 3000 §6–§7 and LLP 3000.007 §6.2, §14, §17 and §18: a receipt keeps
execution identity without historical row content, and residency describes
sources while the shared evaluator decides each answer's completeness.

A named unique collision still carries its original `detail` in the live
refusal. Durable receipt creation removes the field, and historical receipt
decoding clears it defensively. The existing paired revocation observation
now runs with both unnamed and named composite constraints, whose retained
`PRIVATE` column the mutation never supplied; the historical observation
also plants old detail. Four device regressions cover current/historical
receipts on memory/SQLite, drop the first response, reopen the pending
outbox, apply revocation, deliver the retry, persist its terminal receipt,
settle and reopen again. Each also admits a non-colliding write by the new
owner while the revoked reader continues to see no row.

For the completeness finding I chose the narrower, statically proved fact,
horizon-free source coverage. Adding answer-completeness analysis to the
printer would duplicate the evaluator's authorization, truncation and
continuation decisions. Both counterexamples classify every site as Held
and still return `complete: false` with no meter or word cut. The printer
now also requires at least one site, so a constant held query makes no
vacuous coverage claim. The reads card, search card, README and their
existing text assertions agree; no parser form or diagnostic code changed.

## 2026-09-16 — W9R2: reads nested in matching contribute source coverage

Lane W9R2 repairs review N1 on base
`718b188deae72292e74e5c40ccd19b76d65868ef`. The public messages/terms
witness compiles the brief's exact `matching slice('coffee', 0,

residency variants retained only the messages site and printed the positive
coverage line; the runtime still evaluated terms. After the fix, both sites

outside the named ownership paths, changed minimally (3 added lines,

both prefix variants (`Scalar` and `WordPrefix`), `filter` (`where`), all

reads; merge lane setup, lane sources and lane scans already use that
walker. Scan `take` is a literal or named argument with a maximum, so it
cannot contain a read expression. Quarry currently lowers cursors to

skipped scan expression was found.

still distinct from runtime answer completeness.

## 2026-09-16 — Backend-neutral Workroom fixture pack (Astra peripheral lane)

Implemented LLP 3000.009 §10.1's six fixture pieces under
`benchmarks/fixtures/team-workspace/` and `benchmarks/tools/team-workspace/`:
an authenticated loopback email sink, a signed payment provider with fsynced
event/delivery/acknowledgement journals, a SHA-bound fixture extractor,
personas and W3/W5-first starter/conformance actions, a streaming full-scale
action generator with an independent report reducer, and pure React DOM
presentational screens with values/callbacks/test IDs only.

The action adapter registers real accounts and uses normal authenticated
application writes. It persists actual-ID aliases and authoritative receipts,
retries an unknown transport outcome under the same key, and stops before
dependent actions after an unexpected terminal failure. There is no database
import, direct audit insertion, privileged application fixture route or
backend implementation in this pack. All 50,000 large-organization audit

## 2026-09-16 — W10R1: independent job repairs, truthful horizon advice, and integrated recipe coverage

Built against `263495ceb8400e831e6fb43200ecc22276aaa4dc`, the wave-10
integration. The parser now excludes jobs from empty-operation cascade marking:
a retained prelude does not supply a chunk, even when an equality in it needs
a mechanical rewrite. The three regressions cover one prelude binding, a
binding nested inside `if`, and multiple prelude statements. Each default
check now shows both errors. Correcting equality alone still reports the
missing body in all three controls; adding a chunk makes all three compile.
No other cascade path changed.

Replaced the false silence sentence in the sync card, N_NO_HORIZON's code
explanation and the package README. The proposed replacement matches
`needs_whole_partition`: an eligible mutation's held point/rule/aggregate or
insert-proof site can suppress the advice. Kept the bounded-group explanation
and note emission unchanged. Split the wording and behavior assertions so an
incorrect sentence cannot stop the behavior control from running. The same
uncapped public table emits 1 note without a reader and 0 with an eligible
point-reading mutation; the table schema is identical in both programs.

## 2026-09-16 — W10R1b: a follow fits the write ceiling, dev shares diagnostics, excerpts carry content

Base: `263495ceb8400e831e6fb43200ecc22276aaa4dc`. No commit, push, tag,
publication, sub-agent, repository clone or remote machine was used.

Orientation (`llp-orient`): scope is the installed Following recipe, CLI
reporting/fixture loading, cursor advice and their published cards. Governing
LLPs are LLP 3000 §6–§7 and Accepted-as-ruled LLP 3000.007 §14/§18, with
§20.3 for Following, §20.1 for diagnostic discovery, §5.6 for continuation,
and §6.8 for measured fixture residency. These constrain the change to the
existing meter, value model and transaction contract; the cards must compile.
The relevant rationale is atomic promotion and useful help at the failing
site, without turning a missing fixture into a measurement. Open risk:
extra application writes beyond the documented one-edge bridge need their
own promotion allowance. The README, feeds/reads cards and expiry guidance
are updated together. Hand-off: none; the lead owns integration and the
outside-sandbox browser qualification.

The installed backfill is now `max(authors, 200)` capped by
`Ceilings::default().rows_written - BACKFILL_PROMOTION_ALLOWANCE`.
The named allowance is `2 * (51 + 1) + 3 = 107`: two writes per pull route
for the author plus 51 followers, one recipe follow edge, one author-mode
update and one application edge. The unchanged ceiling is 1,024, leaving
917 copied events. The lower clamp retains the earlier 200-event history
window even at `--authors 50`; a separate backfill flag would add another
sizing knob without fixing this transaction limit. The guide's default
loop and README match. Both describe the remaining 83 inbox slots, the
continued 1,000-event source scan and the application's other caps.

The engine regressions use the installed prefixed recipe and the documented
one-mutation app-edge bridge. On the base, the 51st follow aborts at 1,025
attempted writes, and a one-follower delete-and-replace aborts at the inbox's
1,000-row group cap. Both now return `Sent`; the stale deleted-event copy
is still present during the successful replacement, so this is a before-purge
witness. Saturated routes still use the existing recipe behavior.

`check` and dev re-adoption now share filtering, formatting and hidden counts;
`--verbose` reaches the watcher and startup. The dev fixture compares the
whole diagnostic block and count against `check` in both modes, then saves
valid source and confirms generation 2 is adopted. Inline excerpts require
a card paragraph that actually names the diagnostic code; `why` retains its
explicit opening-paragraph fallback. The repeated-refusal positive case uses
`E_QUARRY_TYPE`, and the mixed fixture prints only that dedicated section,
with stable ordering and its own code in the excerpt.

The cap alternative for `N_NO_CURSOR` now requires a nonempty pinned group
and no existing applicable cap. Unscoped and already-capped pages retain
continuation advice; the 9,000-row positive control still traverses all rows
with a cursor. Missing or non-directory fixtures exit 1 before printing a
measurement; directory-entry and fixture-file read errors also refuse.
Init marks both pointer arguments as placeholders. The README lists all five
client/operations sections and routes; its start-path test covers actions,
clock and routes too. All three missing expiry passages distinguish the
application table from server-decided `connected[p]`, which has no expiresAt.
The installed helper list names feedRepost. The three token-sensitive
assertions now compare booleans and use the same redacted message as the
existing wait assertion, keeping actual token strings out of assertion diffs.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Base 51st follow plus app edge | 1,000 requested | 1,160 | 8,634 | 1,025 attempted | E_BOUND; atomic rollback |
| Fixed 51st follow plus app edge | 917 | 1,160 | 8,625 | 1,024 | Sent; 51 follows, 52 routes, 917 inbox copies, 1 app edge |
| Standalone follow, --authors 1008 or 2000 | 917 | 1,005 | 8,259 | 918 | Sent |

Shrinking the copied history saves writes and index work, but not the source
page's examined-row cost: both 200 and 917 copies examine 1,005 rows. The
recipe does not promise unlimited delete/replacement churn before cleanup.

Closed all three coverage gaps without changing their implementations:

- The existing primary-plus-cascade CLI fixture now pins error/excerpt counts
  in all three modes: default 1/0, verbose 2/1, JSON 2/0. This catches counting
  the suppressed cascade toward the inline-help threshold.
- The published `showExpiringRows` function runs inside a real client
  `observe`/`subscribe` lifecycle. A controlled transport drives change-feed
  invalidation and answer replacement; a controlled rendering clock advances
  through the deadlines. Extending at +3,000 ms replaces the +4,500 ms deadline
  with +7,500 ms; the old deadline causes 0 repaints, the new deadline hides
  the row with no replacement answer, a third answer replaces Alice with Bob,
  and unmount leaves 0 render timers and no later repaint/refetch. This is a
  deterministic lifecycle witness, not a browser or wall-clock accuracy claim.
- The existing device suite now executes the reads card's exact typing
  Quarry on SQLite and memory. A server update streams a deadline extension
  from 5,500 to 8,500 ms; each device matches the server and retains 1 row at
  5,500 and 8,499, then 0 at 8,500 without a streamed deletion. The search
  card's exact directory queries run on both stores with `sync public` added
  to profiles for acquisition. Each acquires 25 profiles, returns 0 matches
  for 3 empty/whitespace/punctuation needles, walks browse and search in
  20 + 5 rows each without duplicates, and finds the last profile with `dav`
  from a reset cursor (1 match).

`guide::CODES` using `guide_for`'s default card. This is the actual inline
selector: a code must appear as a whole word in an unfenced prose paragraph;
a heading or fenced example alone does not qualify. Per-site card overrides
are outside this default-route census. Before: **137 registered, 67 with,

## 2026-09-16 — W11a: promotion preserves an existing follower's delivery

Lane W11a (Codex, gpt-6-astra), based on
`e08f1573c08a09e367876eff011ffd9824fee527`. Implements the H1 mitigation in
`benchmarks/runs/2026-09-16-snapback4-clique-astra-0.2.26/friction-review.md`
and records the changed decision in LLP 3000.007 §20.3. This deliberately
changes the intentional shipped saturation policy; it is not a wave-10
regression. The recipe previously committed promotion while skipping a
follower at 32 pulls, leaving that still-subscribed reader without later
posts. Documentation of that loss was not an acceptable product outcome.

The promotion loop now requires every follower's `tryPull` to succeed,
including the triggering reader. `FEED_PROMOTION_PULL_CAP` rolls back the
entire triggering transaction: app and recipe edges, author mode, installed
routes, online counts and delivery changes. The author stays unshared and
all existing readers keep receiving private pushes. The author's optional
self route and own-inbox fallback remain. A direct new follow of an already
shared author still uses `FEED_PULL_CAP`. The feeds card, package README,
code explanations and diagnostic-to-card mapping describe how to act: each
saturated follower must free a shared-author slot, then the refused follow
can be retried with a new write ID. Freeing only the caller's slot cannot
fix a different follower. If those readers cannot free slots, decline the
new follow and preserve pushed delivery. More than 32 shared authors needs
a separate serving design; neither the cap nor the merge width increased.

Tests replace the previous expected-skip policy. The exact reader-first
case fills 32 routes, follows Q while Q is unshared, then adds 49 further
followers before the 50th further follow attempts promotion. A second case
places the one saturated reader last among existing followers, after 49
other follower routes have been attempted. Both compare every stored table
and the sync sequence before/after refusal and require zero committed events.
The next post reaches all 50 existing readers. The 31-slot control promotes

# Feeds: complete Following with a small celebrity merge

Call `register` during profile creation. `follow` and `unfollow` are
idempotent; promotion is permanent and atomic with the follow that triggers
it. Promotion requires a pull lane for every follower, including the triggering
reader. If any follower already uses all 32 shared-author slots,
`FEED_PROMOTION_PULL_CAP` refuses the whole follow/promotion transaction,
including the app edge, author mode, routes and counts. Existing followers
keep receiving private pushes; no follower is silently skipped.

Full card: snapback4 guide feeds

```text
Before: family client — the client refused before asking the server: a hook used outside its provider, a session that ended, a malformed argument. The message says which.
After: family client — the client threw without returning a write or asset outcome. The message includes the original exception; a missing write outcome does not prove whether the server admitted it. Repair the client and collect with the original intent id before issuing another write.
```

## 2026-09-16 — W11R1a: terminal receipts survive another tab's adoption

Codex / gpt-6-astra, lane W11R1a. Base:
`975bbf76e01a9418fe0073cfebb8f9dc999ada3b`. No commit, push, tag or
publication. This entry is one append; all 1,439,958 preceding bytes remain
identical to the base.

The three initial deterministic regressions failed before the implementation:
A adopts and deletes B before C opens, for both sent and failed outcomes;
and a source lock stays held through the completed foreground open, then
releases with no subsequent sync, change-poll reply or backend write. The
first two returned undefined in C; the third never revisited the source.
The real wasm device and backend run under controlled persistence and Web
Locks. These are Node ordering models, not real-browser termination evidence.

Terminal write history now has shared custody. Before an orphan can be
removed, its value-free terminal receipts are committed under a separate
nonwaiting Web Lock into one `${name}:receipts` record. The existing
`WRITE_HISTORY_LIMIT` bounds it to 256 entries. Existing shared ids keep their
outcome and position; successful reads neither copy nor refresh the window.
Every opener and receipt lookup reads the shared window alongside its own
bounded 256-entry device window (at most 512 distinct receipts per lookup).
An adopter no longer copies terminal history into its private device. Shared
persistence failure leaves the source intact. No pending state, arguments,
predictions or historical result values enter the shared record.

The store lock remains the only reliable ownership authority. There is no
separate live/dead signal; a live or suspended owner's lock is never stolen.
The eleven foreground attempts and their sleeps are gone: a pass takes one
nonwaiting attempt per candidate. One one-second timer per opener re-enumerates
busy candidates until they are claimable or the opener closes, with no growing
candidate queue. A recovered outbox notifies ordinary client flushing even
without a backend change. Outbox ownership and original mutation ids remain
exclusive. The published writes card, README, linked client reference and
RFC section 20.4 record the distinction.

Measured controls: forced adoption recovers 1 sent and 1 failed receipt; the
sent write applies exactly once, the failed write zero times. The delayed-release
control records 4 foreground lock misses across separate passes, 0 subsequent
backend writes and 1 application. The outbox control records 0 live-owner
adoptions, 1 adopter, 1 POST and 1 application. Inserting 257 distinct recovered
ids retains 256 receipts in 1 shared record and evicts 1; reads do not refresh
it and a conflicting duplicate cannot change its shared outcome. Two competing
adopters preserve 2 receipts for 2 applications. W5c now forces the survivor's
adoption to complete before reopening, with no timing-based receipt retry loop.
The two acquisition tests for destination windows now check that adoption leaves
local history unchanged while the shared window holds 256 receipts.

cannot establish where a terminal receipt will be found. Persisting terminal
history independently before deleting its source resolves that race; an
independent retry obligation resolves the later release without weakening
exclusive ownership of executable writes.

## 2026-09-16 — W11R2: quiet orphan recovery, reserved recipe refusals, and accurate records

Implemented the four round-2 items against base
`31fdebcc0fcd63f437fc8815a01ea9a22a3741af`, without committing, pushing,
tagging or publishing.

A: busy source and receipt locks now have one cancellable queued Web Lock
request per lock. It wakes recovery after release, on the serialized device
chain; foreground opening does not wait for a live tab to close. An opening
barrier also keeps a release signal from racing initial restoration/adoption.
Evicted and unidentified journal candidates have no retry timer and are left
for a later open or identity/sync signal. Recovery failures exhaust three
backoffs (1, 2, 4 seconds) per open; later sync/open signals may try again.
The persistence adapter has a noncreating existence check. IndexedDB uses
its database list when available and aborts a missing database's creation
transaction in the fallback; journal-only discovery still works without
`indexedDB.databases()`. Receipt reads check existence before reading the
shared window. Round 1's commit-before-delete, shared value-free custody,
immutable duplicate outcomes and 256-receipt window are unchanged.

B: all nine authored refusals in the installable Following recipe now use
`FEED_`. The six renamed codes are CANNOT_FOLLOW_SELF, AUTHOR_NOT_FOUND,
POST_NOT_FOUND, EVENT_REMOVED, ORIGINAL_REQUIRED and NOT_AUTHOR; the three
previously missing explanations are now registered with their own paragraphs.

use the new names. Other applications retain their own generic codes. The
census lexes `else CODE` in the actual installable recipe, independent of the
prefix census, and checks every code's registration, card, dedicated section

C: the README now agrees with the native card and parser: a mutation cannot

## 2026-09-16 — W11INT: reconcile wave 11 and concurrent ownership fixes

Base: `9b288fc08ba581a5ad16d3b1a41a279c7c900729` (0.2.27).
Merged `origin/main` at `04df69bde74e0b17a60d468aa9f500b9b4104e26`, with
merge base `a0d48a4e6b660e2bfca3de3ef3470ef7787f3d15`. The four conflict
contents are resolved; no commit, push, tag or publication was made.

The two ownership mechanisms are complementary. `claimStore` validates the
provider's exact/non-alternate or discoverable `:tab-*` alternate name. The
built-in IndexedDB claim already takes `hold(locks, name)`, so taking a second
Web Lock around it would contend with our own claim. Orphan adoption takes
one validated, nonwaiting provider claim, retains main's namespace guard, and
uses wave 11's cancellable queued Web Lock request as the built-in provider's
release signal. The 20 ms × 10 polling loop is absent. Custom providers with
independent claims retry at open/sync; a free, unrelated browser lock must not
create an immediate recovery loop. The shared receipt window uses that same
validated provider authority, including for memory persistence without Web
Locks. `shareReceipts` still commits before source removal, and every receipt
lookup still reads through the shared window. No receipt returns to exclusive
custody. No value model, meter ceiling or existing corpus case changed.

Main edited exactly the `sync` and `native` cards. Its required audience-column
text and its native memory/fuel/module-binding text now live in the extracted
`guide/sync.rs` and `guide/native.rs`. Inspection also found that wave 11 had
corrected the native boundary sentence in addition to extracting it: its
mutation/prediction/server-replay sentence is retained, matching the README.
The first guide run caught losing that correction (49 passed / 1 failed);
the corrected guide run is 50/50. Both prepended `Revised` histories were
checked against their parents. This journal's earlier content is exactly
ours followed by main's 3,146-byte addition, extracted against the merge base;
that equality was verified before appending this one block. No union merge.

The browser-lock Node fixtures now explicitly use the IndexedDB provider's
claim implementation over memory storage; main's new memory claim has its own
single-realm authority and cannot stand in for a Web Lock release. The added
custom-provider regression runs both with no browser locks and with unrelated
browser locks, preserves a busy source, recovers its receipt after release and
sync, and refuses to claim an out-of-namespace enumeration result. Both cases
pass with zero unrelated waits, foreign claims and timers. The extra manual
file outside the four conflict paths and requested extracted cards is
`packages/snapback4/test/web-durability.test.mjs`; the auto-merged navigation
suite also has the one-line fixture adaptation. Other main changes are imported

## 2026-09-17 — B1b: action-bound identity-session handoff

The existing SQLite `POST /auth/session` path now accepts the bounded internal
`identity-session/v1` binding. In one immediate write transaction it rechecks
the raw bearer by digest as a live service credential for the claiming worker,
reuses the action queue's held/live claim-authority chain, and then either
creates one custom session plus its binding or explicitly recovers a lost
committed delivery. The typed binding row records invocation, intent, the
immutable principal/kind/days digest and values, original expiry, issued
family, and target principal generation. It contains no raw token.

An existing binding never behaves as byte-idempotent delivery. An ordinary
repeat refuses. `replaceLostDelivery: true` requires the current claim, the
original live expiry and target generation, and a still-live issued family;
it deletes every token currently in that family and inserts one replacement in
the same family, capped at the original expiry. Refresh is found through the
family. Logout, logout-all, revocation, expiry, changed inputs, stale or
cross-invocation leases, wrong workers, cancellation and settlement do not
turn the retained binding tombstone into a fresh mint. The unbound legacy
route and its response shape are unchanged.

Focused serial evidence used `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=6` and one test thread:

- `cargo test -p snapback4-core --test bound_session -- --test-threads=1`:
  5 passed, including two actual SQLite connections, concurrent replacements,
  the precheck/revocation window, family refresh and overlap, and every named
  service/admitting/target authority end state.
- `cargo test -p snapback4-core --lib identity:: -- --test-threads=1`: 5 passed;
  `--test identity`: 2 passed; `--test action_context`: 8 passed; and
  `--test work_records`: 6 passed.
- The exact real-HTTP shape/header, recovery, fencing and secret-safe
  diagnostic case passed. An earlier full `serve::tests::` run passed 44/44;
  a final rerun passed 43 and exposed the unrelated 1 ms long-route claim
  timing test, which then reproduced alone. `--test work_records`: 1 passed;
  `--test clock`: 17 passed.
- `cargo test -p snapback4-lang --test guide -- --test-threads=1`: 37 passed.

`./ref-check --verbose` reports 481 LLP documents, 9,034 references in
24,000 files, zero errors and zero unchecked references.

This slice adds no PostgreSQL parity or production claim, generic identity
framework, provider protocol, `contract.ts` change, publication, remote work
or origin contact. C3.1's Postgres receipt semantics are unchanged.

## 2026-09-17 — Route registry synchronization correction

The clean parent `3a337177d7a313a29f433b14661ce1bf43920271` was green in
the supervisor's 3/3 witness, so the earlier attribution of the observed route
registry failure was inconclusive. The test declared a 1 ms route, waited for
the request to return 503, and treated that response as proof that durable
route admission was ready for the registry claim. A pre-admission 503 does not
provide that synchronization.

The repaired witness keeps a real socket route request live under its ordinary
two-second bound, waits until the store contains both durable admissions, and
then requires the registry claim to return exactly the long action and maximum
route names. It settles the claimed route by its actual id and claim session
with an empty 204 `RouteResponse`, then observes that 204 on the original
socket. No product behavior changed.

## 2026-09-17 — B1a OIDC terminal codes survive public action recollection

The action settlement boundary now recognizes exactly the ten terminal codes
emitted by the TypeScript OIDC helper: `E_OIDC_BINDING`, `E_OIDC_CALLBACK`,

## 2026-09-17 — B1b review repair: exact bound entry and serialized logout

The B1b HTTP boundary no longer chooses legacy minting merely because a
`binding` object is absent. Either a `binding` key or any
`x-snapback-action-lease` header selects the exact bound wire form. The full
body, binding, principal, kind, days, authorization header and single nonempty
lease header are parsed and validated before the engine mutex; malformed or
one-sided bound attempts refuse without minting. Only requests with both
signals absent retain the legacy defaults and coercions. Integer days retain
the existing 1–3,650 clamp in both lanes. The response is produced only after
the short engine guard has dropped.

HTTP logout now authenticates the presented token as live and closes its
refresh/recovery family within one immediate SQLite writer transaction. Thus a
logout committed first leaves the existing binding tombstone unable to
resurrect the family, while a lost-delivery replacement committed first makes
the old bearer stale: logout returns 401 `E_AUTH` and leaves the replacement
live. Logout-all generation semantics, action-session authority checks, and
the lower-level close used by other internal boundaries remain unchanged.

## 2026-09-17 — B1d.1 trusted OIDC profile binding checkpoint

The existing private OIDC handoff now supplies one additional required
`principal` argument to the configured `transactions.verified` mutation. The
helper derives it from the already-validated issuer and subject with the same
internal `oidcPrincipal` function used by session minting. It does not use the
admitting guest, callback/client claims, email or application provider input,
and it adds no public context or session capability. The generic exported
transaction row and begin payload remain unchanged: profile order, proof time
and stored principal are recipe-private fields.

The managed recipe assigns a monotone login-start order through a private
service counter and stamps proof start with managed `now` inside
`identityBegin`. `identityVerified` checks the claimed completion, refuses a
changed issuer/subject/principal on repeat, records the transaction settlement
and conditionally upserts one trusted profile keyed by the derived principal in
the same interpreter transaction. Existing profiles must retain the same
issuer/subject. A delayed lower-order completion settles its own transaction
but cannot replace newer profile evidence; an equal-order replay must match the
same login, timestamps and email evidence. The fixed recipe policy expires
email evidence five minutes after the original begin stamp, at a strict
`proofExpiresAt > now` query boundary, so replay cannot refresh proof age.

Only a present bounded provider email with `email_verified: true` is eligible.
A newer false, missing or unverified value replaces older evidence and clears
eligibility; a later valid login can change it again. Equal email across two
issuer/subject principals creates two profiles and never links them. Profile
rows are service-written, readable only by their own principal or the recipe
service, and grant no membership. There is no editable verification field,
email uniqueness, identity auto-link or provider-revocation synchronizer.
Login-start order is explicitly not provider email-change chronology.

A pre-B1d verified-write receipt lacks the new required principal and therefore
has different mutation input. Existing input binding must refuse its old write
id; there is no migration, backfill or new receipt marker, and the documented
recovery is a fresh login/action invocation. The existing mint step name and
input, bound-session protocol, discovery phases, cancellation behavior and
recovery fence are unchanged.

## 2026-09-17 — C3.3: PostgreSQL authority fact transaction parity

The experimental PostgreSQL layout is now exactly
`snapback4-postgres-evaluation-3`. Creation atomically adds the complete
SQLite-shaped `_principal_generations`, `_sessions` and `_requests` facts and
their equivalent indexes. Identity values remain lexical text, time and
generation values are signed 64-bit integers, family and authority fields stay
nullable, and `cancelled` is a non-null boolean defaulting false. Opening exact-
matches v3 and refuses both v1 and v2; there is no migration, ALTER, backfill or
silent adoption path.

The real Postgres transaction now implements the existing typed
`AuthorityTransaction`: generation with zero fallback, exact digest and latest
live family reads, all ten authority work fields by id or nonunique claimed
digest, exact-token invalidation and whole-family invalidation. Shared fact and
policy cases run unchanged over SQLite and PostgreSQL. They retain lexical
identity, `COALESCE(family, token_digest)`, strict expiry/lease/deadline
boundaries, refresh lifetime distinct from admitted expiry, legacy NULL family,
all three partial authority combinations, generation and parent revocation,
multi-hop delegation, cycles, principal/owner/digest/state mismatches and
service generations. Adapter mapping is tested separately from policy.

Borrowed PostgreSQL walks use the existing repeatable-read/read-only
transaction. Both invalidations refuse before mutation in read-only and
Serializable transactions; only a transaction that already holds the
serialized shared-head fence may execute them. A real two-connection witness
establishes a repeatable-read snapshot, commits a newer family member through a
separate serialized/head-fenced transaction, proves the old snapshot remains
stable, then proves a reopened snapshot sees the commit. A rolled-back session
stays absent after reopen. Future identity/work writers must acquire the head
fence before sampling their injected clock; this checkpoint adds neither a
clock nor a public writer API.

## 2026-09-16 — W12a: rolling ranking is a live read, not a sweep-index omission

Investigated the engine before building and chose outcome (b), recorded in
LLP 3000.007 §20.21. The expiry sweep already removes the source, subtracts
its physical aggregate contribution, updates every target index and appends
partition events in one transaction. Its runner uses unbounded ceilings;
source count is bounded explicitly to 2,000 per host pass, scanned in batches
of at most 256. A value index would cost two extra entries per surviving
aggregate change and one on group deletion, with no extra target row write
or source scan. The SQLite/MemoryRows experiment measured 2,000 changes,
4,000 rank-entry writes and three entries on final deletion (two base, one

## 2026-09-16 — W12b: public writable copies of maintained aggregates

Added `N_PUBLIC_AGGREGATE_COPY`, a note at the copied column, under
LLP 3000.007 §20.20. The signal is an actual direct scalar maintain read in
an insert/update/upsert field in a declared program or helper, including a
job. A public/read-allow or publicly synced target must have a provably
unrestricted update rule, and the column must be mutable. Copies are
reported once per table/column/maintain. A matching name, type, group key,
increment, alias or arithmetic expression is not evidence. Simple boolean
unrestricted equivalents are covered; this is deliberately not a general
rule prover or data-flow analysis. No error, mechanical fix, authority,
meter ceiling or serialized form was added.

The note describes latent table permission accurately: a principal still
calls a declared mutation, not arbitrary table writes. It names the copied
aggregate, says that the update rule lets any principal set the public
column through a mutation, and recommends reading the maintain directly or
restricting the update rule, with insert authority checked too. Its dedicated
feeds-card section is pinned verbatim, its code is registered, and the README
names the discovery path and limits. The guide census is 156 registered codes,
156 dedicated sections, zero missing.

## 2026-09-17 — B1d prerequisite: transaction-local token hashing

Quarry now has exactly one `sha256(text)` spelling. It accepts one required
present text value (including empty text), infers `text <=64`, and returns the
lowercase hexadecimal RustCrypto SHA-256 of the exact UTF-8 bytes without
normalization, case folding, quoting, salt, key, entropy or a host callback.
The new IR variant runs only in the shared Rust interpreter used by the server
and devices; existing serialized builtin spellings and the conformance corpus
are unchanged.

Before hashing, the interpreter charges the step meter by the input UTF-8 byte
length plus one with checked `usize` conversion and addition. It then charges
the fixed 64-byte owned `Value::String` through the existing heap convention.
The builtin is absent from prediction's total-expression allowlist and is
conservatively refused by conditional write-target purity. Existing residency,
presence, hidden-row metering and rule authorization remain controlling; the
presence regression proves a presence-selected hash keeps `predicts: never`.

Tests pin empty, ASCII, non-ASCII, composed and decomposed UTF-8 vectors,
non-normalization, unary arity, wrong and optional type refusal, and the inferred
output bound. Meter cuts distinguish the pre-hash variable step refusal from
the fixed result allocation: a scalar query step cut refuses E_BOUND, a heap
cut returns null and incomplete, and a mutation cut rolls back an earlier
insert. The focused device witness produced the same output through the shared
interpreter on the SQLite and memory-backed device stores and the SQLite server.

Focused serial evidence used `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=6`, the existing repository
Cargo, `--locked`, and one test thread:

- `snapback4-core --test meter`: 8/8;
- `snapback4-core --test corpus`: 18/18 harness tests, 211 Rust-server cases
  passed and 83 named skips; its Postgres arm reported 294 skips because the
  feature was disabled;
- the focused language SHA-256 regression: 1/1;
- the language guide suite: 50/50;
- the language presence suite: 9/9; and
- the focused device witness: 1/1, run once over each of SQLite and memory.

One broader `frontend_regressions` attempt ran all affected tests successfully
but ended 37/38 because the existing Bun workspace dependencies were absent for
its emitted-TypeScript test. The diagnostic requested `bun install
--frozen-lockfile`; no install was performed under this slice's prohibition,
and the directly affected filtered test then passed. No real PostgreSQL harness
was run: its focused tests require an explicitly supplied isolated local server,
and compilation alone is not claimed as host evidence.

This primitive is only for high-entropy capability tokens and content
checksums. It is not password hashing, low-entropy email anonymization, a
signature, a MAC, entropy generation or permission to publish digests
indiscriminately. No invitation schema, issuance or acceptance recipe, auth
endpoint, raw-token persistence, client-contract field, JavaScript transaction,
static admission ceiling, dependency, version, publication or deployment is
included. No root inventory, full suite, benchmark, network, remote, origin,

fault proxy. The historical actual run `682a834d5` completed its primary

instrument retained no raw error cause, this repair does not claim that
intentional engine teardown caused that failure.

The proxy now retains the phase in which each request began. Unexpected
failures from proof-origin requests remain fatal even when observed after the
teardown transition. Once all primary assertions and the two-stream secrecy
check finish, the harness checks the existing first-failure latch, explicitly
enters expected teardown, refuses newly arriving polling/background traffic
with an empty 503, and gives existing proof requests a bounded 30-second drain
while the engine remains live. It then closes proxy connections before
stopping the engine. Drain, close, server, protocol, request and three custody
failure categories produce fixed phase/category codes only; no exception
message, path, URL, header or body enters output. The intentional committed-
reply cut is the single narrow proof exception. A preexisting material failure
is never cleared or replaced, and observations are appended only after clean
proxy and engine teardown.

The inseparable owned-child cleanup now recognizes signal termination as
terminal, subscribes before signalling, bounds both TERM and KILL waits, and
never selects a process except through the existing exact owned-child object.
The private scratch retention, actual mint cut, UID/start/ancestry custody
checks, external mandatory five-minute ProcessCustody envelope, provider-count
assertion and unknown-failure fail-closed output are unchanged.
